The secular facility offers a wide variety of programs, including yoga, pickup sports, and music classes, as well as food preparation classes and food assistance programs. To ensure that it met the needs of the community – including a large percentage of new Canadians, visible minorities, and families with limited disposable income – leaders and church volunteers collected data from nearby residents, local politicians, and social services over a multi-year planning period. The staff and volunteers work to build a place where everyone feels welcome and supported, from recent immigrants learning to cook new meals for their children to teens finding confidence on the basketball court. SideWalk welcomed over 14,000 visitors in 2024, its first year – then matched that number in the just first half of 2025. Most of the funding for the SideWalk Centre came from the sale of a portion of the church’s land to a residential developer, with additional financial support from local funders such as the Hallman Foundation. Having a development project already underway helped streamline the zoning and approvals for the community centre, and the new building was soon “shovel ready.” The Church made a deliberate choice to dedicate the majority of the funds from its congregational donations to support building and operating the Centre, putting lasting infrastructure in place for a safe, productive community space.

All Saints’ Anglican Church in Waterloo, Ontario, purpose-built the [SideWalk Community Centre](https://www.allsaintswaterloo.ca/programs/sidewalk-community-centre) as part of an extensive redevelopment of its property to provide one of the only in-neighbourhood community centres in the city. The creation of the community centre stemmed from the realization that there was a lack of spaces for recreation and connection in this rapidly changing neighbourhood with a large percentage of new Canadians, visible minorities, and families with limited disposable income. To ensure that it met the community’s needs, leaders and church volunteers collected data from nearby residents, local politicians, and social services in interviews and conversations over a multi-year planning period.
 
 The secular SideWalk Community Centre offers a wide variety of programs, including yoga, pickup sports, music classes, and cultural events, as well as food preparation classes and food assistance programs. The staff and volunteers work to build a place where everyone feels welcome and supported, from recent immigrants learning to cook new meals for their children to teens finding confidence on the basketball court. Opened in 2024, SideWalk welcomed over 14,000 visitors in its first year – then matched that number in the first half of 2025. More than half of attendees were children and teenagers. The high usage rate is evidence that the centre is meeting a community need, particularly for youth and immigrants.
 
 Most of the funding for the SideWalk Centre came from the sale of a portion of the church’s land to a residential developer, with additional financial support from local funders such as the Hallman Foundation. Having that development project already under way helped streamline the zoning and approvals for the community centre, and the new building was soon “shovel ready.” The Church made a deliberate choice to dedicate the majority of the funds from its congregational donations to support building and operating the centre, putting lasting infrastructure in place for a safe, productive community space.

 The robust church community at All Saints’ provides a steady volunteer and donation base that assists in everything from running the food bank to hosting fundraising events that generate supplies for the programs, such as sports balls and cookware. By thoughtfully repurposing property at All Saints’ Anglican Church and listening to local voices, community champions and church volunteers created an essential community amenity in the SideWalk Community Centre. Their example demonstrates how churches can fill gaps in “third places” and strengthen community life at the neighbourhood level.

- It is important to have a passionate community champion who dedicates time and effort to driving the mission of the project forward through all phases of the process, from planning to development to execution. Planning for a leader in the next generation, to continue community commitment and programming at the site, will ensure long-term sustainability and impact of the project. 
- Having a clear, written guide or checklist for adaptive reuse projects would make the process more accessible for a broad range of community champions. In particular, navigating zoning, site plans, and by-law surprises can be daunting for those who are not developers or planning practitioners. 
- Talking to neighbours, social agencies, sports organizations, and potential funders from the outset is important to identify community needs and gaps, and to build support before major decisions are made. While the staff of a community centre may be small, consistent outreach and a clear mission invite people to contribute time, skills, and resources, allowing for a great deal to be accomplished on a limited budget. 
- Obtaining written commitments from groups that will use the space helps reassure donors and grant makers that the project will have lasting impact. SideWalk’s success came from connecting with 13+ agencies, ranging from food security programs to basketball clubs.
The SideWalk Community Centre on the property of All Saints’ Anglican Church has become a much-needed “third place” for a rapidly changing, diverse neighbourhood in Waterloo.

In 2023, the [Community Sector Council of Newfoundland and Labrador](https://cscnl.ca/about/) (CSCNL) launched the Social Innovation Lab and its flagship pilot, the [Social Enterprise Through Acquisition](https://www.socialinnovationlab.ca/social-enterprise-through-acquisition-seta) (SETA) program, to preserve small businesses while diversifying revenue streams for community organizations. SETA connects community organizations with businesses available for acquisition in rural Newfoundland and Labrador to ensure that these businesses continue to serve their communities. Potential buyer organizations can access up to $15,000 to cover transition-related costs. They also receive one-on-one assistance throughout the process. The program supports a variety of acquisition models, including full business purchases, worker co-operatives, and transfers of specific assets, such as equipment or facilities. The SETA program helps business owners by playing a confidential matchmaking role, identifying buyers who share similar values through outreach and partners such as community business development corporations, and creating profiles for prospective buyers. To ease organizational strain on community organization buyers, CSCNL also aims to connect them with wage subsidies, student placements, and newcomer employment programs – or, in some cases, to facilitate acquisitions that include existing employees. For community organizations that are not yet ready to venture into acquisition, CSCNL offers revenue diversification training (the Thriving Non-Profits program) in partnership with Scale Collaborative and the Community Foundation of Newfoundland and Labrador. CSCNL demonstrates how social enterprise models can preserve critical services while building long-term resilience. Succession planning, often treated as a private matter, can instead be a powerful tool for community development, economic stability, and social innovation.

The approaching “tsunami” of potential small business exits – as founders approach retirement without a succession plan – presents an urgent challenge for rural communities. Many small businesses are deeply embedded in local economies, and their loss could undermine employment, access to essential goods and services, and community cohesion. At the same time, community organizations (including non-profits, charities, co-ops, and social enterprises) are being asked to do more with fewer resources. 
 
 The [Community Sector Council of Newfoundland and Labrador](https://cscnl.ca/about/) (CSCNL), a registered charity dedicated to the support of community entities in the province, has developed an innovative response. In 2023, CSCNL launched the Social Innovation Lab and its flagship pilot, the [Social Enterprise Through Acquisition](https://www.socialinnovationlab.ca/social-enterprise-through-acquisition-seta) (SETA) program, to preserve small businesses while diversifying revenue streams for community organizations. SETA connects community organizations with rural businesses available for acquisition to ensure that these businesses continue to serve their communities. Potential buyer organizations in rural Newfoundland and Labrador can access up to $15,000 to cover transition-related costs. They also receive one-on-one support throughout the process. The program supports a variety of acquisition models, including full business purchases, worker co-operatives, and transfers of specific assets, such as equipment or facilities. 
 
 The SETA program helps business owners by playing a confidential matchmaking role, identifying buyers who share similar values through outreach and partners such as [Community Business Development Corporations](https://www.canada.ca/en/atlantic-canada-opportunities/services/community-futures.html), and creating profiles for prospective buyers. To ease organizational strain on community-organization buyers, CSCNL also aims to connect them with wage subsidies, student placements, and newcomer employment programs – or, in some cases, to facilitate acquisitions that include existing employees. For community organizations that are not ready yet to venture into acquisition, CSCNL offers revenue diversification training (the Thriving Non-Profits program) in partnership with Scale Collaborative and the Community Foundation of Newfoundland and Labrador. 
 
 Since its launch, the program has supported three new social enterprises with several others in progress. In Port Rexton, the Two Whales Coffee Shop was converted into a worker co-op that preserved the business and its place as a community hub for locals and tourists. In central Newfoundland, a non-profit organization acquired a taxi service to integrate affordable transportation into its programming and address the lack of accessible transportation options in the region. In Stephenville, the Mi’kmaw Cultural Foundation has acquired a building that will become a child-care social enterprise and community hub. 
 
 Newfoundland and Labrador has a strong culture of community, which helps enable this work. At the same time, challenges persist. Business owners may hesitate to disclose succession plans, transactions can take months to finalize, and community organizations often face limited capacity to take on new enterprises. Financing is another barrier, as grants can be restrictive while traditional loans are rarely well suited to the needs, governance, and structures of community organizations. Some of the resources necessary to complete an acquisition are dependent on external providers – potentially delaying the process. 
 
 CSCNL addresses these issues by leveraging a growing network of partners – from legal and financial professionals to social finance providers like GoParity and Fairlead – to guide acquisitions and assemble capital. One-on-one communication helps build trust with sellers, while relationships with government reduce bureaucratic delays.

Photo credit: CSCNL](/local-solutions/web-assets/spotlighted-solutions/11/TW_Launch.jpg "Co-op members who acquired the Two Whales Coffee Shop in Port Rexton, N.L., preserving its legacy as a vibrant community gathering place. Photo credit: CSCNL") 

 By de-risking acquisitions, fostering cross-sector partnerships, and tailoring solutions to local contexts, CSCNL demonstrates how social enterprise models can preserve critical services while building long-term resilience. Succession planning, often treated as a private matter, can instead be a powerful tool for community development, economic stability, and social innovation.

- Policy support, accessible funding, and committed leadership are critical to creating the legal, financial, and mentorship infrastructure buyers and sellers need. 
- In-person engagement and visible commitment to supporting local businesses and the community are essential for overcoming resistance, building trust, and ensuring smoother transitions. For example, CSCCL hosted meetups in rural communities with local organizations, co-creating opportunities for community well-being. It also engaged directly with community organization boards to accelerate decision-maker buy-in and address buyer constraints. decision-maker buy-in and address buyer constraints. 
- Flexible tools – such as structured legal frameworks, customizable funder-ready business plans, and a range of financing instruments – help reduce risk and expand financing options for non-profits and social enterprises. 
- Building networks of aligned social partners and adapting approaches to local contexts strengthens the impact of community organizations and small businesses. Holding realistic conversations about time and capacity helps ensure their long-term sustainability.

The small communities of Bruce and Grey Counties have been hit hard by Canada’s decades-long opioid epidemic. Opioid cases and death rates soared during the COVID-19 pandemic and still haven’t returned to pre-2020 levels. In response, a team of paramedics and community health workers has built a nimble, compassionate model for addictions-related health care in the community. The [Supportive Outreach Service](https://unitedwayofbrucegrey.com/sos-helps/) (SOS) grew from a May 2021 crisis in Hanover, Ontario, where a COVID-19 outbreak in a rooming house led to over 50 residents being quarantined, many with mental health and addictions issues and little in the way of personal support networks. For weeks, various local agencies collaborated to meet their needs on-site, asking few questions and providing health care as well as other necessities such as regular meals, hygiene supplies, counselling, and even shoes.  The infected residents recovered – and general health indicators of the group had also improved significantly, with many later entering addictions treatment programs. Today, SOS responds to calls seven days a week across Bruce Grey with a similar “no wrong doors” approach – meaning that when someone seeks help through any point of contact, SOS prioritizes their immediate needs and connects them to a range of supports. Its teams provide medical care, harm reduction equipment, vaccinations, crisis management, and supportive addictions treatment aligned with patient goals. In a region with no public intercommunity transit and few private bus carriers, SOS meets patients where they are, through mobile clinics and home visits, rather than asking them to travel to facilities when in crisis.

Today, SOS responds to calls seven days a week across Bruce Grey with a similar “no wrong doors” approach – meaning that when someone seeks help through any point of contact, SOS prioritizes their immediate needs and connects them to a range of supports. SOS is led by Grey County Paramedics and the United Way of Bruce Grey, in partnership with the Canadian Mental Health Association – Grey Bruce and with Brightshores Health System. Its teams provide medical care, harm reduction equipment, vaccinations, crisis management, and supportive addictions treatment aligned with patient goals. In a region with no public intercommunity transit and few private bus carriers, SOS brings support to where patients are, through mobile clinics and home visits, rather than asking them to travel to facilities when in crisis. 

SOS staff prioritize visibility in, and connection with, the community. Free Naloxone kits hang outside their office and are refilled as people take them. SOS holds bi-weekly pop-ups at markets in Owen Sound and Hanover to answer questions and provide Naloxone training. It works: most of Bruce Grey’s unhoused residents have heard of the service through word of mouth. 

SOS relies on partnerships with public agencies and other organizations along the continuum of care, seeking to supplement, rather than duplicate, their work. It sets clear boundaries, asking police to give them a “wide berth” so clients can get support without fear of police presence. Local police services have confirmed that SOS’s work has reduced emergency call volumes. 

Staff at SOS humanize patients as community members and tie their well-being to that of the community. One approach has been to highlight how harm reduction helps prevent disease transmission by mitigating risks like shared needles and unsafe supply. Another initiative offered grocery cards to community members who cleaned up needles from parks, creating visible improvements without punitive measures. 

SOS is supported by the Ontario Health Team, community paramedic funds, micro-grants from Grey County, and United Way fundraising. In October 2025, federal funding allowed the service to expand mobile operations from four to seven days a week. Challenges remain: a lack of affordable housing makes patient progress hard to sustain. Provincial policies like closing safe consumption sites and reducing addiction treatment supports hinder harm reduction efforts. Even so, the success of SOS has led to other communities seeking to adapt the model, having demonstrated that health care that meets patients where they are is not only possible but necessary.

- Programs like SOS help paramedics provide immediate care without needing to send patients to the ER. Local paramedics may already have similar programs that can be scaled up with increased support.  
- Community presence builds trust and buy-in. It can be a net benefit to sacrifice in-office staff hours for field work that makes an organization’s programming more effective and popular. 
- Compassionate programs like SOS require economic and housing resources for patients to transition out of care. Medical interventions are more effective when patients are not also surviving economic precarity. 
- Local champions, who may include health workers, patients, and family members, are essential. Many have stories that humanize the opioid epidemic and show how these efforts create change.
United Way of Bruce Grey brings a wide range of services and information into the community, hosting pop-ups at markets.

Patients often pass through siloed organizations that struggle to coordinate care, information, and resources. The consequences can range from frustration at the challenge of navigating resources to re-traumatization if patients must recount their experiences at each intake. Health care providers interact with different funding streams and privacy laws from all levels of government, which can discourage and complicate collaborations. [Converge Mental Health Coalition](https://www.convergementalhealth.org/) formed in 2022 to help improve coordination and data sharing among providers. Starting in Alberta with six members, Converge now has over 100 members across multiple provinces and sectors. After interviewing mental health providers across Alberta about their challenges, Converge developed its [Information Sharing Framework](https://www.convergementalhealth.org/our-work/what-is-the-information-sharing-framework) (ISF), which reframes the sharing of information, often seen as a risk, to be a benefit to organizations – even an obligation, since it can improve patient care. The ISF helps providers identify partner organizations, applicable regulations, reasons for collaborating, and the type(s) of collaboration needed to achieve their goals. Converge’s work helps organizations understand and navigate their place within the response. Information sharing has great potential to reduce administrative burdens and the duplication of work at organizations that are often stretched thin. [Converge Mental Health Coalition](https://www.convergementalhealth.org/) formed in 2022 to help improve coordination and data sharing among providers. Starting in Alberta with six members, Converge now has over 100 members across multiple provinces and sectors. After interviewing mental health providers across Alberta about their challenges, Converge developed its [Information Sharing Framework](https://www.convergementalhealth.org/our-work/what-is-the-information-sharing-framework) (ISF), which reframes the sharing of information, often seen as a risk, to be a benefit to organizations – even an obligation, since it can improve patient care. The ISF helps providers identify partner organizations, applicable regulations, reasons for collaborating, and the type(s) of collaboration needed to achieve their goals. 

For example, a public agency may seek counselling support for a patient. Recommending a partner clinic might require no information sharing at all. But a patient who will be working with both the agency and the clinic going forward could benefit from the two having an ongoing relationship that includes sharing detailed information about the patient’s medical history and progress. 

The ISF can help clarify for an organization how legislation governs its work, and how it can shift its practices for beneficial data sharing, including sample documents such as consent forms and information sharing agreements. The change is not always quick: organizations may have a mental picture of how they operate and hesitate to adapt for collaborations. Because small organizations often have little capacity to adjust their practices and add new staff responsibilities, large organizations may need to set up information sharing systems to support their smaller partners. 

Looking ahead, Converge’s main goal is to help more organizations adopt the ISF, providing ongoing support for adopters and setting up communities of practice. While some adopters appreciate the ISF’s comprehensive detail, Converge is working on making the framework easier to implement for those who prefer a “plug-and-play" approach. It is also adapting the ISF for other provinces, starting with Ontario, and finding many similarities across provincial privacy legislation. Converge also recommends policy changes to facilitate beneficial information sharing, some of which have been adopted in Alberta legislation. One such adopted change is improved safety clauses governing when organizations can disclose information in emergencies. 

The serious challenges of mental health issues have reached a crisis level in Canada; Converge’s work helps organizations understand and navigate their place within the response. And challenges arising from a diverse, fragmented patchwork of providers are not unique to mental health – Canadian service providers in many areas lack resources and rely on others to fill in their gaps, making information sharing a necessity. Information sharing has great potential to reduce administrative burdens and the duplication of work at organizations that are often stretched thin. Implementing it well is easier said than done, but for a growing number of organizations, Converge makes doing so easier.

- Information sharing should be tied to a specific purpose for patients rather than conducted for its own sake. Limited partners need less information than closely integrated core partners. 
- Organizations should evaluate the role of their interventions in each patient’s well-being. Developing appropriate information sharing practices with partners can build trust, better align everybody’s work, and improve patient care. 
- Organizations often face crisis points that pit legal obligations to disclose information against the unclear expectations of partners. Transparent up-front preparation can ensure organizations don’t erode trust with patients and partners.

Converge Mental Health Coalition helps organizations coordinate care, share data, and improve outcomes through its Information
Sharing Framework.

In 2019, the City of Edmonton launched the [Affordable Housing Investment Program](https://www.edmonton.ca/programs_services/funding_grants/affordable-housing-investment-program) (AHIP) to address urgent funding gaps and catalyze affordable housing development and rehabilitation. The AHIP positions the City as the first investor in affordable developments, providing up-front support that allows housing providers to mitigate risk and attract additional funding at the provincial or federal level. For every dollar the City contributes to the program, it secures approximately four more from other governments. The AHIP was designed to be flexible, aligning with changing federal and provincial priorities. Its evaluation criteria mirror those of the CMHC Co-Investment Fund, making it easier for projects to compete across multiple funding sources. A housing reserve account provides funds pre-approved by Council, so City staff can negotiate quickly with provincial and federal government partners – and can reallocate money annually in response to shifts in those higher-level government programs. Since its launch, the program has distributed more than $125 million and supported the creation of over 2,400 affordable units. Edmonton’s stock of social and affordable housing has grown by nearly 33%, from 13,536 units in 2019 to over 18,000 in 2025. The AHIP positions the City to achieve its long-term goal of residents having access to affordable housing in all parts of the city.

In Edmonton, a 2023 City-led needs assessment revealed that nearly 50,000 households are in core housing need. Through consultation with local housing providers, the City found that one of the biggest barriers to building affordable housing was pre-development risk. Non-profit providers often had to assume significant up-front costs without dedicated funding, making it difficult to reach the stage where provincial or federal investment could be secured. This uncertainty stalled many otherwise viable projects. 

In 2019, the City of Edmonton launched the [Affordable Housing Investment Program](https://www.edmonton.ca/programs_services/funding_grants/affordable-housing-investment-program) (AHIP) to address urgent funding gaps and catalyze affordable housing development and rehabilitation. The AHIP positions the City as the first investor in affordable developments, providing up-front support that allows housing providers to mitigate risk and attract additional funding at the provincial or federal level. For every dollar the City contributes to the program, it secures approximately four more from other governments. 

The AHIP was designed to be flexible, aligning with changing federal and provincial priorities. Its evaluation criteria mirror those of the CMHC Co-Investment Fund, making it easier for projects to compete across multiple funding sources. And a housing reserve account provides funds pre-approved by Council, so City staff can negotiate quickly with provincial and federal government partners – and can reallocate money annually in response to shifts in those higher-level government programs. 

Partnerships are at the heart of the program. The units built under it are given to local non-profit housing providers and social service agencies, ensuring they remain affordable. Federal and provincial contributions, combined with political support from Council and the Mayor, have ensured sustained funding and momentum. The City has also worked closely with Indigenous partners, adjusting its intake process and increasing its maximum contribution for Indigenous-led projects from 25% to 40% to reflect the unique challenges the Indigenous community faces with accessing equity. 

Since its launch, the program has distributed more than $125 million and supported the creation of over 2,400 affordable units, compared to just 720 units five years earlier. Edmonton’s stock of social and affordable housing has grown by nearly 33%, from 13,536 units in 2019 to over 18,000 in 2025. The AHIP positions the City to achieve its long-term goal of residents having access to affordable housing in all parts of the city.  

To complement the AHIP, Edmonton has adopted various housing-enabling tools, including a number of zoning reforms: removing parking minimums, allowing up to 8 units as of right on certain lots, and making affordable and single-room occupancy housing permissible throughout the city. The municipality also provides discounted land to housing providers, offers grants and exemptions to lower the property tax burden, and has hired a dedicated safety code officer to help manage affordable housing projects after construction. Despite these measures, challenges remain: affordable housing, particularly supportive housing, faces systemic barriers; delays in multi-government funding create lost opportunities; and community resistance persists. [Public education](https://www.edmonton.ca/programs_services/housing/welcome-homes?utm_source=virtualaddress&utm_campaign=welcomehomes) and a city-wide target of 16% affordable housing per neighbourhood help mitigate opposition, underscoring Edmonton’s municipal leadership. 

Other municipalities are already looking to Edmonton as a model. Calgary’s [Housing Incentive Program](https://www.calgary.ca/social-services/funding/affordable-housing-incentive.html) and, at the provincial level, the Alberta [Affordable Housing Partnership Program](https://www.alberta.ca/affordable-housing-partnership-program) draw on Edmonton’s experience. With AHIP’s success, Canada’s most northern provincial capital has significantly expanded its affordable housing supply while building a model that is both scalable and replicable across Canada.

- Investing early, leveraging other funding, and pairing financial support with policy reform are all key aspects of the program’s success. 
- The City frames housing as essential infrastructure, a human right, and an economic growth strategy, sustaining political will and a dedicated municipal budget. 
- Moving from one-off approvals to portfolios of projects could unlock further operational efficiencies, reducing costs and speeding delivery. 
- Conversations are underway about creating a streamlined “one-stop” funding portal where all levels of government approve projects simultaneously. Such a system would cut through bureaucracy, reduce delays, eliminate risk, and accelerate timelines.

[Brique par Brique](https://www.briqueparbrique.com/) is a non-profit organization established in 2016 to respond to rapid gentrification and displacement in Parc-Extension, one of Montreal’s most diverse neighbourhoods. The organization operates under a dual mandate of building affordable community housing and spaces and cultivating collective action and local leadership through community development and cultural programming. To obtain capital funding for its work, Brique par Brique launched its first community bond campaign in 2018, raising over $360,000 in nine months from 40 community investors. Community bonds are guaranteed fixed-rate bonds provided by a community issuer to a non-profit borrower. They offer an innovative pathway for non-profit and community-led housing providers to finance projects in a way that keeps wealth within communities and strengthens community organizing. Funds raised from the bonds can then be used for site acquisition and development, to leverage additional funding, or to pay down higher-interest debts. With these funds and some additional support from the Government of Québec through the (now-abolished) AccèsLogis program, Brique par Brique acquired land and is constructing a 31-unit social housing complex with the aim of renting out units by 2027 at 25% of household income or less. They also used some of the funds to open a cultural centre in 2021. Community financing offered Brique par Brique a launchpad for its affordable housing project, as well as an opportunity to build relationships with community investors and create support for future social-purpose projects.

To accomplish these goals, Brique par Brique needed to find capital. Traditional financing is expensive and often unavailable to smaller non-profit housing providers. Further, the private sector has different aims from community-led housing, where value is defined by the social and equity implications of providing housing as a human right rather than for profit. There is also often fierce competition among housing providers for limited public sector funding, which is not nearly plentiful enough to cover the need for affordable and social housing across Canada.

Running a community bond campaign builds relationships with like-minded community investors, but requires significant resources and time. To mount a successful campaign, organizations must first educate community members about what community bonds are and how they work, then maintain communication consistently throughout the lifespan of the project. Brique par Brique found that, although its investors were aligned with the organization’s solidarity values, many felt frustrated by how slow the site acquisition process was. The organization’s staff needed to host one-on-one meetings with the investors to offer transparency and rebuild trust. 

Despite these challenges, Brique par Brique has launched a second community bond campaign in 2025 to raise $5 million for two new projects: a community centre, and a second solidarity housing project in Parc-Extension. The organization received a $100,000 grant from CMHC in 2019 to [document](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/6435a471274088074467609d/t/67e5a81fb739be1b67630884/1743104032470/Force_collective_de_levier_logements_abo.pdf) its community bond model and other findings from the first acquisition. Community financing offered Brique par Brique a launchpad for its affordable housing project, as well as an opportunity to build relationships with community investors and create support for future social-purpose projects.

- To run a community bond campaign, an organization needs to be prepared to hire, train, and dedicate significant team capacity. Staff need to be able to conduct effective values-based outreach to find aligned individuals, educate potential investors about community bonds as a financial tool, maintain consistent correspondence with investors, and keep investors engaged for future initiatives.  
- There is a need for more sustainable financing tools that allow community-led organizations to more readily access low-cost, lower-barrier funds; the current options are labour-intensive and difficult to scale. Discussions in the sector have included these two possibilities, among others: 
    - pooling community bonds and other funds for social-purpose projects into a ready debt market for borrowers to access; and 
    - creating a secure alternative certification for checking and verifying borrower credentials that allows a wider range of organizations to access funds.

The [Killick Ecovillage Co-operative](https://killickecovillage.ca/) in Portugal Cove-St. Phillip’s, N.L., is a cohousing village that has worked to address many of the challenges that smaller communities face when creating a Community-Led Housing (CLH) project. Founders combined resident investment, grants, and external financing to build a shared foundation for the project. Resident investment in the village makes the project unique among CLH models available in Canada. While traditional models such as co-ops and CLTs provide residents with decision-making power in the development of their community, the residents are still leasing the land from a larger organization that manages ownership. Members of the Killick Ecovillage, in contrast, will have long-term leases on their own homes, with the autonomy akin to home ownership, as part of Canada’s first Mutual Home Ownership Society (MHOS). At Killick, the governance model is intended to foster continued community engagement. From its inception, the resident community was shaped through a participatory design process, with workshops that invited brainstorming and discussion about the members’ ideal future together. This shared governance framework sustains community decision-making while ensuring that operations, services, and long-term plans remain aligned with the community’s values and needs.

Once built, the village will be a 51-home sustainable, multi-generational, mixed-income community. The project began with a group of individuals with a vision who pooled resources to buy a 58-acre heritage farm and are planning to build a 9-acre housing development.  

Most public funding streams for CLHs are geared toward larger projects, and so were not a fit for Killick. Instead, the founders combined resident investment, grants, and external financing to build a shared foundation for the project. Resident investment in the village makes the project unique among CLH models available in Canada. While traditional models such as co-ops and CLTs provide residents with decision-making power in the development of their community, the residents are still leasing the land from a larger organization that manages ownership. Members of the Killick Ecovillage, in contrast, will have long-term leases on their own homes, with the autonomy akin to home ownership, as part of Canada’s first Mutual Home Ownership Society (MHOS). 
 
Based on a successful framework imported from the United Kingdom, a MHOS is a CLH model in which residents collectively own their properties – an approach that disconnects occupation of the property from its land value, protecting the houses from losing affordability with market fluctuations. At the Killick Ecovillage, the community carries a single mortgage. Each household contributes a resident share with a minimum loan component of $15,000 and pays an all-in-one community fee that is capped at 35% of household net income. Because contributions are scaled to income, higher-income residents help subsidize housing costs, making it more affordable for others. At the same time, there is a cap on the loan amount, creating an incentive for higher earners to pay off their loans quickly once they reach the limit, after which they can earn interest on their balances. Residents can choose from homes at different price points, with less expensive homes resulting in smaller loans and faster payoffs.  

At Killick, the governance model is intended to foster continued community engagement. From its inception, the resident community was shaped through a participatory design process, with workshops that invited brainstorming and discussion about the members’ ideal future together. Today, residents continue to guide the evolution of the co-op through consensus-based decision-making. They collectively identify needs and assign people to take on internal roles, such as waste management, food production, or maintenance; where additional expertise is required, they decide as a group whether to hire external support, often pursuing grants to offset costs. This shared governance framework sustains community decision-making while ensuring that operations, services, and long-term plans remain aligned with the community’s values and needs.

Construction is a major driver of greenhouse gas emissions (39% globally), with cement production alone accounting for about 8% of global carbon dioxide output. The construction industry also faces deep labour challenges: many workers encounter mental health and safety risks, while women and other underrepresented groups remain largely excluded from leadership positions in the trades. [Tooketree Passive Homes](https://www.tooketree.com/), a modular housing developer based in Muskoka, Ontario, was founded in 2018 to address both of these issues, as well as the high cost of housing. Central to the Tooketree model is the development of [sustainable, ecological, efficient, and durable (SEED) panels](https://www.tooketree.com/seed), which sequester carbon and insulate the building so that it uses 90% less energy to heat and cool than a conventional home. The standardized design allows Tooketree to guarantee fixed pricing and deliver homes with higher energy performance than typical site-built construction, where efficiency features are often cut to save time and money. To date, Tooketree has sequestered 105,000 kg of carbon through SEED panels, created nearly 56,000 hours of living-wage employment, and delivered 65 housing units. Since 2022, it has provided nearly 5,000 hours of on-site training to Indigenous women and employed more than 30 women in trades. Tooketree’s is helping to reshape the construction industry into one that has a lower carbon footprint, is more inclusive, and prioritizes collaboration. By proving that sustainable, affordable housing can also strengthen local economies and diversify the labour force, Tooketree demonstrates that tackling the housing crisis and the climate crisis can – and must – be pursued together.

Toronto and Region Conservation Authority (TRCA) created the [Sustainable Neighbourhood Action Program](https://trca.ca/conservation/sustainable-neighbourhoods/) (SNAP) to improve the sustainability and resilience of older neighbourhoods in the Greater Toronto Area, many of which face challenges in stormwater management, home retrofits, or water and energy conservation. By better connecting neighbours, government agencies, and other stakeholder groups, the program encourages sharing knowledge, improves planning efficiencies, builds implementation partnerships, and explores opportunities for expanded impact. The result is accelerated progress toward solutions rooted in local priorities and conditions – place-based interventions focused on ensuring older urban neighbourhoods are resilient, sustainable, and vibrant. To select neighbourhoods for the program, TRCA uses geographic information software (GIS) tools to identify hotspot areas with overlapping priorities, such as flood risk, socio-economic vulnerabilities, and residents with mobility challenges. Once a project is underway, the SNAP approach involves a heavy investment in relationship building, and as a result TRCA has become an innovator in community-led engagement and collaborative implementation. The organization identifies the unique interests and priorities of each neighbourhood – for example, community safety, access to green space, or resilience to heat – and tailors its approach to reflect local voices. Since 2009, SNAP has revitalized 17 neighbourhoods across 14 municipalities in the Greater Toronto Area, touching nearly 250,000 residents. It has also inspired municipal policy shifts, scaling local action into broader urban sustainability and climate resilience strategies.

Working alongside local governments and conservation authorities, NAI provides ecological and economic expertise to support the identification, valuation, and integration of natural assets into financial planning and asset management. NAM measures value through the services that natural assets provide, including water filtration and flood mitigation, carbon sequestration, and even recreational benefits that would otherwise require built infrastructure. Many cities have institutionalized NAM results into municipal policy and take natural assets and natural infrastructure solutions into consideration when drafting community plans and climate adaptation strategies. Ontario has integrated NAM into provincial regulation via O. Reg 588/17, which requires all 444 municipalities in the province to include green infrastructure in their asset management planning process.

Working alongside local governments and conservation authorities, NAI provides ecological and economic expertise to support the identification, valuation, and integration of natural assets into financial planning and asset management. Its approach, which supports low-cost, sustainable service delivery through natural infrastructure, is making NAM a mainstream, standardized practice across Canada. 

NAM measures value through the services that natural assets provide, including water filtration and flood mitigation, carbon sequestration, and even recreational benefits that would otherwise require built infrastructure. The valuation process may also consider the cost to restore natural assets if they become depleted as a minimum baseline value. Non-market benefits, such as cultural significance, may need to be considered qualitatively – there are some things that do not have a price, and dollar figures do not represent nature’s intrinsic value.  

The process of mapping, valuing, and managing natural assets often involves cross-departmental collaboration at the local level with engineers, accountants, and environmental staff. In addition to municipalities, NAI has also worked with several First Nations aiming to use natural asset inventories to inform their decision-making about infrastructure projects. Incorporating Indigenous perspectives and knowledge about natural assets can also contribute to other reconciliation efforts at the local level, as it involves recognizing and accounting for cultural values specific to the natural features of the area.

The CityHive [CityShapers in Schools](https://www.cityhive.ca/programs/cityshapers-in-schools) program is a four-session classroom-based workshop series for grades 5–12 that challenges students to think more deeply about climate action, housing affordability, and public space design. By connecting students to governance, civic engagement, and city planning processes within their schools and neighbourhoods, the program uses local issues to nurture their curiosity and give them the tools to make their voices heard in civic processes. The program is offered for free or on a sliding pay scale to public schools throughout the Metro Vancouver region, giving priority to communities that have historically been under-represented in municipal politics and that experience greater barriers to civic participation. The workshops are designed in consultation with certified teachers and co-led by a CityHive educator and a youth leader. Local government staff and elected officials are a key component of the program’s success, and CityHive works with municipalities on a fee-for-service basis to provide student input directly into open engagement projects. Over 300 students have met with municipal staff and elected officials to learn about and engage with such planning projects as the Squamish Nation Climate Action Strategy, the North Vancouver Active Transportation Plan, and the Clayton Corridor Skytrain Expansion Plan. There are few opportunities for young people to learn the skills they need to practice positive civic engagement. Many school districts have shifted to a generalist curriculum that aims to provide a well-rounded education but does not give students local context or include a locally rooted civic education. Since 2016, the Vancouver-based non-profit CityHive has been working to address these gaps by running civic educational programming across the province. The CityHive [CityShapers in Schools](https://www.cityhive.ca/programs/cityshapers-in-schools) program is a four-session classroom-based workshop series for grades 5–12 that challenges students to think more deeply about climate action, housing affordability, and public space design. By connecting students to governance, civic engagement, and city planning processes within their schools and neighbourhoods, it uses local issues to nurture their curiosity and give them the tools to make their voices heard in civic processes. 

The program is offered for free or on a sliding pay scale to public schools throughout the Metro Vancouver region, giving priority to communities that have historically been under-represented in municipal politics and experience greater barriers to civic participation. The workshops are designed in consultation with certified teachers and co-led by a CityHive educator and a youth leader (aged 18–30). The CityShapers team works to ensure the program curriculum is robust and inclusive, collaborating with Indigenous elders and knowledge keepers, architects, urban planners, and researchers from local universities to ensure the program is rich and engaging. Accessibility is at the core of the approach, with a modular curriculum designed from the perspective of students. The program incorporates different learning styles through activities such as games, urban design mapping, and democratic process simulations. It is tailored to each unique classroom, and regularly revised and improved based on student feedback.  

Local government staff and elected officials are a key component of the program’s success, and CityHive works with municipalities on a fee-for-service basis to provide student input directly into open engagement projects. Over 300 students have met with municipal staff and elected officials to learn about and engage with such planning projects as the Squamish Nation Climate Action Strategy, the North Vancouver Active Transportation Plan, and the Clayton Corridor Skytrain Expansion Plan. Many students continue to follow projects after the classroom component ends, as the experience has helped to build a sense of agency and connection to issues that affect their communities. 

 ![Students discuss local issues in a CityShapers classroom program. Photo credit: CityHive](/local-solutions/web-assets/spotlighted-solutions/64/CSinSchools.png "Students discuss local issues in a CityShapers classroom program. Photo credit: CityHive")  

CityShapers has grown from 1,025 participants in the 2022/23 school year to 1,450 (across five school districts) in 2024/25. It now has a waiting list. Participating students describe how the program has contributed to a new sense of understanding about sustainability, city policy, and civic affairs, and made them feel more confident and competent in providing feedback to municipal leaders – and each other. The CityShapers program addresses the need for local context in teaching about civic affairs and the importance of young people contributing to their cities and communities as engaged and thoughtful residents. Individual projects and electoral cycles are short, but educating students in sustainability, inclusion, and justice will have long-lasting effects.

- The curriculum is modular and can be tailored to a particular grade level and specific local issues. By collaborating with interested teachers, its frameworks can be scaled across the district, province, or country to reach more young people and their communities. 
- Opportunities to learn about and participate in local civic engagement should not depend on a school’s resources; keeping this curriculum free or low-fee is essential. 
- Building more links with ongoing development projects in the area can increase the impact of young voices in how civic projects shape cities and communities while also providing opportunities for partnerships and funding.

Communities are exploring alternative, safer ways to travel to school through [bike bus programs](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H5S8c_rgxIY), which organize and schedule times for children to bike to school alongside parent or teacher volunteers. Parents map routes, repair bikes on the way, and invite other families to join. A highly visible critical mass on the street, including a protective barrier of adults, discourages risky behaviour from drivers. This encourages active transportation for vulnerable road users and fosters a sense of community. Communities can also form walking buses for kids using walkers, wheelchairs, and other mobility devices. Bike buses typically operate weekly from the middle of September to the end of October, resuming after March Break – although a warming climate and cheaper equipment are making winter riding more feasible. Bike buses exist across Canada, including two in Toronto (in Davenport and Scarborough) established with the help of Toronto’s “[Bicycle Mayor](https://www.ctvnews.ca/toronto/article/first-unofficial-bicycle-mayor-of-toronto-hopes-to-make-cycling-safer-and-more-accessible/)” alongside a coalition of biking groups, non-profits, and parents. The programs require only minimal funding for basic supplies like safety vests and repair kits. Wider community support is critical. Parents rely on principals to help coordinate with school staff and encourage students to join, addressing opposition with proactive empathy by emphasizing the goal of creating safe spaces for the community’s kids. Advocates point out that bike bus programs will have been truly successful when they are not needed, because the city streets are safe enough for cycling children as a matter of course.

Every morning during the school year, over 5 million Canadian students make the trip to class – and most of them, thanks to the combination of car-first street design and school policies, are dropped off by a parent in their car. This routine transforms the public spaces and streets surrounding schools across the country into places where collisions and injuries are more likely for everyone. Some communities, however, are exploring alternatives through [bike bus programs](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H5S8c_rgxIY), which organize and schedule times for children to bike to school alongside parent or teacher volunteers. A highly visible critical mass on the street, including a protective barrier of adults, discourages risky behaviour from drivers. Parents map routes, repair bikes on the way, and invite other families to join. Communities can also form walking buses for kids using walkers, wheelchairs, and other mobility devices. These encourage active transportation for vulnerable road users and foster a sense of community. 

Bike buses typically operate weekly from the middle of September to the end of October, before resuming after March Break – although a warmer climate and cheaper equipment are making winter riding more feasible. Bike buses exist across Canada, including two in Toronto (in Davenport and Scarborough) established with the help of Toronto’s “[Bicycle Mayor](https://www.ctvnews.ca/toronto/article/first-unofficial-bicycle-mayor-of-toronto-hopes-to-make-cycling-safer-and-more-accessible/)” alongside a coalition of biking groups, nonprofits, and parents. The programs needed minimal funding for basic supplies like safety vests and repair kits. But it was critical for them to have support from the wider community. Parents relied on principals to help coordinate with school staff and encourage students to join. The opposition that came from some quarters, such as parents who preferred driving directly to school and neighbours concerned about traffic impacts, was addressed with proactive empathy by emphasizing the goal of creating safe spaces for the community’s kids. 

Goodwill and community champions are not enough to make these programs sustainable. Bike buses can lose momentum when supportive principals and teachers transfer to other schools or when parents disengage during school breaks. They need more volunteers to accompany them when cities lack permanent, safe bike infrastructure along routes to school. In Toronto, they are constrained by provincial efforts to remove bike lanes even as they are all the more necessary in light of broad policy targets for climate action and safe transportation.  

Advocates point out that bike bus programs will have been truly successful when they are not needed, because the city streets are safe enough for cycling children as a matter of course. On the way to that goal, bike bus initiatives show how bicycling can become a normal, joyful part of growing up in Canada if we’re willing to let go of the wheel.

- Enthusiastic support from parents and school principals is essential for starting a bike bus in a community. Because they require very few funds, the main challenge is building political will and community support. 
- School boards and the Ontario Ministry of Education can make it easier for communities to launch these initiatives through formal policies, micro-grants for basic supplies, and cohesive messaging. 
- Bike buses demonstrate the value of permanent biking infrastructure by showing how excited kids are to bike along their routes when it is safe. Communities can link their bike bus programs to city strategies for public safety, transportation, and climate action to get support.

Many young people across Canada face barriers to accessing education and employment, particularly in remote, rural, and Indigenous communities, which can affect their long-term well-being. The Tamarack Institute sought to address these challenges through its [Communities Building Youth Futures](https://www.tamarackcommunity.ca/networks-for-change/youth-futures) (CBYF) network. From 2019 to 2024, it developed the network and implemented programming in 20 communities across 11 provinces and territories. At its core, the initiative provides young people with opportunities to shape local youth support strategies themselves. Rather than giving convening responsibility to existing staff, CBYF compensated local youth for taking on these roles, leading community engagement initiatives, and co-creating solutions with adults. The resulting strategies went beyond traditional employment and educational programs to support young people holistically, including their basic needs, mental health, and cultural identity. Tamarack acted as an intermediary between each community and the federal government, providing a backbone of funding, facilitation, and capacity building throughout the program. It also took on the administrative work of reporting, which allowed community organizations to focus on program implementation. CBYF’s multi-year funding enabled hiring at least one full-time employee in each community, mentored and supported by the CBYF program staff, to build skills and experience. Youth often have ideas for how to address challenges in their own communities, but may lack the support and resources to make substantive change. Initiatives like the CBYF model demonstrate ways to engage them not as subjects of policy, but as active agents with the knowledge and skills to shape it.

Many young people across Canada face barriers to accessing education and employment, with results that can affect their long-term well-being, particularly in remote, rural, and Indigenous communities. The Tamarack Institute, an anti-poverty non-profit operating throughout Canada, sought to address these challenges through its [Communities Building Youth Futures](https://www.tamarackcommunity.ca/networks-for-change/youth-futures) (CBYF) network. From 2019 to 2024, it developed a network and implemented programming in 20 communities across 11 provinces and territories, focusing on those that have a significant youth NEET population (people aged15–29 not in education, employment, or training). 

At the core of this initiative was providing young people in these communities with opportunities to shape local youth-support strategies and initiatives themselves. Rather than giving convening responsibility to existing staff, CBYF compensated youth for taking on these roles, leading community engagement initiatives, and co-creating solutions with adults. The resulting community strategies went beyond traditional employment and educational programs to support young people holistically, including mental health, mentorship, community and cultural identity, and basic needs. Strategies included free after-school programming, drop-in spaces with employment resources, and summits for youth leaders. In Portage la Prairie, the community created a “Roving Campus” for students at risk of not completing high school: introducing alternative credits, providing lunches, and meeting students where they were after learning that unreliable transportation and food insecurity were major barriers. With support from the school board, the campus is now integrated into the local school system and expanding into another CBYF community (Digby, N.S.) with financial support from the Rideau Foundation. 

Funding was provided by Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC). Together with Tamarack, ESDC identified the first 12 CBYF communities based on their large NEET populations and the communities’ readiness to engage in youth-led collaborative change efforts. Tamarack acted as an intermediary between each community and the federal government, providing a backbone of funding, facilitation, and capacity building throughout the program. It also took on the administrative work of reporting, which allowed community organizations to focus on program implementation. Once each community had established priorities with Tamarack’s support, it applied for an annual one-year grant from ESDC to implement and scale its solutions, drawing on Tamarack’s extensive poverty reduction resources. CBYF’s multi-year funding enabled hiring at least one full-time employee in each community, mentored and supported by the CBYF program staff to build skills and experience. 

Serious challenges remain. Among the 12% of Canadian youth who are NEET,  roughly a quarter are caring for children, and over a third are looking for paid work. Indigenous youth are disproportionately represented. Youth barriers are reflected in adulthood disparities; for example, 42% of Indigenous adults have educational attainment at or below a postsecondary level, compared to 25% of non-Indigenous adults, a symptom of ongoing inequities. Ten years have passed since the Truth and Reconciliation Commission included “equitable access to jobs, training, and education opportunities” among 94 Calls to Action that largely remain unfulfilled. 

Tamarack continues to facilitate a network that connects CBYF participants with one another, sharing success stories, new ideas, and opportunities for funding and youth employment. Youth often have ideas for how to address challenges in their own communities, but may lack the support and resources to make substantive change. Initiatives like CBYF model demonstrate ways to engage them not as subjects of policy, but as active agents with the knowledge and skills to shape it.

- Non-profits can act as intermediaries between under-resourced communities and federal funding. Tamarack built infrastructure for local leaders that took on many of the burdens of federal funding (such as reporting tasks), while providing access to existing resources, expertise, and connections to peers in other communities. 
- Providing compensation for community members who participate in initiatives ensures that they can remain involved over the long term. For youth, participation also provides access to mentors and experience. 
- CBYF provided the initial funding and support that let communities build successful policy interventions based on Tamarack’s [Collective Impact](https://www.tamarackcommunity.ca/collective-impact-toolkit) framework; communities were then able to leverage these successes for funding outside of ESDC.
The CBYF annual gathering brings participants and leaders together for learning and inspiration.

Vancouver is the first major city in Canada to institute a mandatory [community benefit agreement](https://www.buysocialcanada.com/learn/community-benefit-agreement/) (CBA) policy, after years of advocacy from community stakeholders including Buy Social Canada. The policy, which applies to developments over 45,000 square metres in size, requires that developers demonstrate their best effort to reach three targets: 10% local employment, especially of members of equity-seeking groups (inclusive employment); 10% local procurement (from within Vancouver); and 10% social procurement (from verified social impact or equity-seeking businesses). Projects must continue to practice social procurement and inclusive employment throughout their operations. The New St. Paul’s Hospital redevelopment, owned by Providence Health Care, is the first project to trigger the City of Vancouver’s CBA policy. Buy Social Canada is the CBA’s independent third-party monitor, overseeing compliance and supporting its success. Since construction started in 2023, the New St. Paul’s Hospital redevelopment has generated nearly $100 million in social procurement spending and $200 million in local procurement spending. Beyond the dollars flowing into the local and social economies, Buy Social Canada is using this first major project to develop networks, demand, and, eventually, capacity in the social enterprise community. Buy Social Canada is striving to make the New St. Paul’s Hospital redevelopment, and by extension the Vancouver CBA policy, a clear and transparent model for other projects and cities to follow. Following its iterative and aspirational approach to advocacy and policy development, places across Canada can build on this momentum to create local social returns on development investment.

Vancouver is the first major city in Canada to institute a mandatory community benefit agreement (CBA) policy, after years of advocacy from community stakeholders including Buy Social Canada. The policy, which applies to developments over 45,000 square metres in size, requires that developers demonstrate their best effort to reach three targets: 10% local employment, especially of members of equity-seeking groups (inclusive employment); 10% local procurement (from within Vancouver); and 10% social procurement (from verified social impact or equity-seeking owned businesses). Projects must continue to practice social procurement and inclusive employment throughout their operations. With the CBA policy in place creating demand for local and social purchasing, Buy Social Canada is now supporting the next step: equipping local and social businesses with the tools to respond and deliver. Recognizing that developing this capacity is a process, the 10% targets across the three areas are intended to be realistic but aspirational. 

The New St. Paul’s Hospital redevelopment, owned by Providence Health Care, is the first project to trigger the City of Vancouver’s CBA policy. Located in the False Creek Flats neighbourhood, the hospital is scheduled to open in 2027. Buy Social Canada is the CBA’s independent third-party monitor, overseeing compliance and supporting its success. Since construction started in 2023, the New St. Paul’s Hospital redevelopment has generated nearly $100 million in social procurement spending and $200 million in local procurement spending. While the project generally met or exceeded the 10% targets in 2023 and 2024, the need for more specialized construction caused this number to dip in 2025. Moving from basic construction to more advanced and hospital-specific finishings meant there were fewer opportunities to source the right equipment, materials, and expertise locally and from social enterprises.

Beyond the dollars flowing into the local and social economies, Buy Social Canada is using this first major project to develop networks, demand, and, eventually, capacity in the social enterprise community. It works with contractors on the purchasing side, training them in compliance reporting and suggesting ways to fulfill the CBA requirements. It also hosts quarterly meetings and roundtables to connect purchasers with suppliers, identify project needs, and link employers with workforce development organizations. Outside of the project, Buy Social Canada works to certify, and to build capacity in, social enterprises that may then become suppliers for future CBA projects. 

The New St. Paul’s Hospital Redevelopment project has sparked a number of success stories through its CBA commitment. EMBERS Staffing Solutions, CleanStart Property Services (profiled in this chapter), and the Binners’ Project – all social enterprises (certified by Buy Social Canada) that employ individuals facing barriers to employment – won multiple contracts on the project after delivering high-quality work on initial engagements. Through these partnerships, over 200 people accessed on-the-job training, and many found longer-term jobs with subcontractors on the project. Providence Health Care’s partnership with Binners’ Project has also resulted in New St. Paul’s Hospital becoming Canada’s first zero-waste medical facility, with conversations ongoing to continue this partnership in operations. 

Buy Social Canada is striving to make the New St. Paul’s Hospital redevelopment, and by extension the Vancouver CBA policy, a clear and transparent model for other projects and cities to follow. Following its iterative and aspirational approach to advocacy and policy development, places across Canada can build on this momentum to create local social returns on development investment.

- Supply takes time to catch up to demand. The first step after convening public, private, and community partners under a CBA is to begin building relationships and establishing a network. When all parties are willing to learn and iterate together, small-scale local and social suppliers and employees can, over time, develop the expertise and capacity to meet demand from purchasers.  
- Third-party monitors with a dedicated mandate to train and build capacity within the local ecosystem are key to a mandatory municipal CBA policy’s success. They are able to dedicate resources to train, engage, and connect all actors in the ecosystem.

Seeking a new venue where its teaching, research, and performance could connect meaningfully with the public, Carleton University embarked on a unique collaboration with a historic former church to build an off-campus performing arts facility in downtown Ottawa. In 2018, the university acquired property from the former Dominion-Chalmers United Church and created an innovative tenant agreement that allowed the church to continue hosting some services and programming for the community while the university gained access to a unique and beautiful space. The [Carleton Dominion-Chalmers Centre](https://carleton.ca/cdcc/) (CDCC) now serves as Carleton’s arts, performance, and learning centre – a vibrant academic and cultural hub used for lectures, workshops, panels, conferences, and interdisciplinary events, often hosted in partnership with community groups. Beyond university programming, CDCC is a vital space for Ottawa’s arts and non-profit sectors, hosting concerts, classes, meetings, festivals, and special events. Its arts programming includes Ottawa Chamberfest, the Ottawa Children’s Theatre, and the Ottawa Symphony Orchestra, among others. As many universities struggle with reduced enrollment, and churches struggle with deferred maintenance and declining congregation attendance, this partnership is a solution that benefits both while keeping vibrant, often historic, spaces in use. With the CDCC, Carleton has created a welcoming multidisciplinary home for learning and the arts that enriches the student experience while fostering an inclusive space for community programming.

Mabelle Avenue in Central Etobicoke is a dense, low-income, and historically underserved neighbourhood with a very diverse population, including many new Canadians. Like many suburban communities based around towers, Mabelle Avenue lacks access to parks, community centres, and cultural spaces, and its outdoor areas are often neglected and underused – even as rapid new development has increased the need for social connection in the area. For the past 18 years, [Mabelle Arts](https://mabellearts.ca/mabelle-park-transformation) has worked alongside local residents, artists, and architects to raise over $3.5 million and co-create a unique community park that fosters connection, creativity, and belonging: Mabelle Park, which opened in October 2024. What makes this initiative special is its transformation of an overlooked space owned by Toronto Community Housing into a vibrant community hub that responds directly to the needs of this high-density, low-income community. The first park in Canada designed specifically to the needs and desires of lower-income tower residents, Mabelle Park offers a space for residents to connect with nature and with their neighbours, and creates opportunities for social connection through events and workshops. Ongoing park care – such as gardening and maintenance – is often undertaken by community members, which not only fosters stewardship but also supports economic development and employment opportunities, making the park a place for community building and resilience.

The Ritson and Olive Commons Placemaking Project addresses the long-standing challenge of vacant public land by transforming an unused site at 350 Ritson Road South in Oshawa into a lively, community-driven space. This regionally owned property has sat dormant as one of several parcels purchased for future road work – an approach that left gaps in the neighbourhood fabric. The site is located within a neighbourhood that faces significant social and health challenges, including higher rates of poverty, unemployment, and low educational attainment compared with other Durham Region communities and the provincial average. Residents wished to bring some life to the spot until it was needed for other uses. Through a competitive design process, a local artist created murals celebrating pollinators, while new amenities – picnic tables, shade sails, a public book-sharing box, and thoughtfully designed green infrastructure – invite people to gather, read, and relax. Developed collaboratively with those living in the area, the initiative emphasizes authentic engagement, strong partnerships, and solutions rooted in local priorities and assets. Launched in June 2025 under Durham Region’s new Public Art and Placemaking Program, the project shows how a creative temporary use can generate pride and engagement without requiring a major capital investment.

In the Rideau/Vanier neighbourhood of Ottawa, a network of social service organizations has transformed the decommissioned Rideau High School into a vibrant centre for connection, learning, and support. [The Rideau Community Hub](https://rideaucommunityhub.tracottawa.ca/) is a centralized resource located in a community facing high rates of inequality, food insecurity, social isolation, and persistent poverty. Managed by the Ottawa-Carleton District School Board, it hosts around 30 non-profit organizations that provide childcare, a food bank, immigration resources, after-school programs, vaccinations, Indigenous cultural services, supports for seniors, and entrepreneurship training for newcomers. It employs 150–200 people and serves up to 500 visitors each day, building community cohesion and strengthening the local social fabric. The Hub offers versatile spaces that include a 700-seat auditorium, a black box theatre, a full gymnasium, a cafeteria, a children’s play area, two soccer fields, and a community garden. And it strengthens social infrastructure, bringing residents together for cultural, recreational, and health-related programs while improving access to essential services, supporting small business development, and fostering a stronger, more inclusive community.

The role of churches in community life is evolving, and Trinity-St. Paul’s United Church in Toronto, like many places of worship, has increasingly needed to rent out space for programming and performances to generate enough revenue to keep its doors open. Located in the Annex neighbourhood, Trinity-St. Paul’s is an affirming congregation that is heavily involved in activism and the arts. By renting to 60 community groups and booking numerous special events, its Centre for Faith, Justice and the Arts provides an important service to the wider community while balancing the books – but the church has much less space available to run shelters and food services. As another way to extend help to those in need, Trinity-St. Paul’s created a [Community Resources Booklet](https://drive.google.com/file/d/13yYAcc-WOsK50mtngK09P_0qatYgjVD1/view?ia=web) that outlines available services, shelters, food, help lines, and other social assistance groups and locations in and around the neighbourhood. The booklet also connects people who want to help with organizations that are in need of volunteers. The church’s staff undertake the daunting task of keeping this ever-changing list of resources up to date and making the booklet available both on site and in nearby locations. In future, they plan to turn this into a network that matches available spaces and volunteers with those seeking services.

With guidance from the community, the Vanier BIA in Ottawa turned a little-used parking lot into the [Vanier HUB](https://vanierhub.com), a community space for events and programming. It began with a public art project – [painting a mural on a shipping container](https://www.ktsoy.art/vanier) – in 2021, and quickly drew strong community interest, confirming that a simple, accessible venue could spark new life in the area. Support from the My Main Street grant program allowed the lot to be redesigned as a more permanent feature, and the HUB has become a vibrant local anchor, drawing people to the area to shop, learn, and connect through programming centred on arts, culture, sports, and community engagement. Events are designed for a wide range of residents, including francophone, Indigenous, and newcomer communities, and keeping families, youth, and 2SLGBTQ+ participants in mind. The aim is to foster inclusion and a sense of belonging. In 2023 the project won the Downtown Achievement Award of Excellence from the International Downtown Association. The HUB is at the centre of the city’s larger Montreal Road revitalization project, a major streetscape redesign that will add a number of new safety and artistic elements, transforming the area once complete. By turning an underutilized site into a lively gathering place, the BIA has boosted traffic to Vanier’s main street, reframing how the neighbourhood is seen and building pride among residents.

[ActivateYYC](https://activateyyc.calgarycommunities.com/) is a micro-grant program designed to help community associations, businesses, not-for-profits, and individuals bring placemaking and tactical urbanism projects to life across Calgary. The program encourages people to transform untapped neighbourhood spaces into vibrant, people-focused places by providing resources for temporary, low-cost, and engaging interventions in the range of $500 to $5,000. Placemaking projects funded by ActivateYYC include murals, “paint the pavement" projects, public space infrastructure such as seating – and anything else citizens can creatively imagine for their community. Over the years, ActivateYYC has grown consistently, supporting more than 40 projects from new and repeat participants and expanding its annual funding from $60,000 to $400,000. They have secured $2.85 million for the next three years to expand the program further and establish a placemaking innovation lab. Funding comes from the City of Calgary, and the Federation of Calgary Communities is an overarching support organization and civic partner. The program’s adaptable model has proven especially vital during periods of social disruption, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, by strengthening neighbourhood connections and activating public spaces. Through micro-grants and hands-on interventions, ActivateYYC continues to foster community creativity, engagement, and a shared sense of place across Calgary.
