Like many downtowns across the country, Downtown Victoria has experienced many challenges since the arrival of the pandemic in 2020 – challenges that threatened its vitality as a cultural, economic, and social hub for the Greater Victoria region. Even after restrictions eased, the high cost of living, a worsening housing crisis, and mental health and addiction issues, combined with enduring work-from-home patterns, reduced the number of visitors to the core. Many local businesses struggled with rising costs and declining revenue streams amid public perception of higher crime and lack of safety, leading to historic retail and commercial vacancies. The City of Victoria responded by creating the [OUR DWTN Program](https://www.victoria.ca/community-culture/arts-culture/our-dwtn). Initiated in 2023 and funded through an increase in paid parking revenue, the program prioritizes safety, cleanliness, activation, and beautification in the downtown area. Enhanced lighting improves security in darker areas, and around-the-clock street cleaning keeps public spaces tidy. A forthcoming Storefronts program will encourage arts and culture activations in vacant spaces, while public art, seasonal lighting, and horticultural displays enhance the area’s vibrancy and appeal. Together, these placemaking efforts are helping to restore confidence in Downtown Victoria, creating a safer, cleaner, and more vibrant core that supports local businesses, fosters community connections, and celebrates the city’s cultural and economic heart.

Urban alleyways are often neglected spaces that can make pedestrians and adjacent property owners feel unsafe. The Rainbow Ramblas initiative in Calgary is a pilot project to reimagine the city’s alleys as welcoming, multi-functional spaces: it promotes comfort and safety through increased public presence and new uses by adding features such as murals, plants, and inviting street furniture. The project is a collaborative effort between the University of Calgary, municipal leadership, and a number of industry partners. Supported by the Calgary Downtown Association and the City of Calgary’s Downtown Strategy team, this pilot forms part of the broader Green Alley Project (GAP), which is tied to the city’s Greater Downtown Plan. While not intending to displace vulnerable populations, Rainbow Ramblas activates alleys while preserving their service functions, repositioning them from back-of-house zones to front-facing, people-oriented places of creativity, culture, and walkability. Launched in summer 2025, the project includes a pre- and post-installation study to measure impacts on pedestrian activity, visitation, and public life, while building a business case for pedestrianized alleyways.

Across Canada, there remains a profound gap in accessibility when it comes to our built environment. Even though more than 8 million Canadians over age 15 live with disabilities, many workplaces, health centres, recreational facilities, and spiritual spaces remain out of reach. [The StopGap Foundation](https://stopgap.ca/) advances accessibility and builds community through advocacy, education, and hands-on action, providing customized ramps, workshops, and partnerships to remove physical barriers and inspire inclusive design. Since its inception, the organization has eliminated thousands of single-step obstacles across Canada, facilitating greater independence and community participation for people with mobility challenges. Through workshops, talks, and social media, StopGap also educates the public about accessibility, highlighting challenges faced by people with disabilities and our shared responsibility to address them. Their colourful ramps, built in partnership with volunteers, builders, and businesses, remove barriers and spark vital conversations about inclusion. They collaborate with policy-makers, planners, developers, and property owners to embed accessibility into design and maintenance, advancing long-term change.

[Downtown London Trails](https://www.downtownlondon.ca/trails/) is a creative initiative to increase foot traffic in the city’s central core, with the goals of strengthening economic vitality and raising consumer awareness of downtown businesses. The program offers a variety of themed trails – such as “Bakery and Patisserie,” “Crisp Days and Cozy Nights,” “Music and Arts,” and “Holiday Experiences” – with each one highlighting a selection of businesses in downtown London. Using Bandwango software, the BIA adds businesses to an interactive digital map where consumers can sign up, check in at different locations, and earn points toward prizes such as downtown merchandise and gift cards. To ensure a successful experience, the BIA also gave businesses training and support. While at first it was a challenge to get businesses to participate in an unfamiliar program, direct outreach and positive testimonials helped build momentum. By 2024, the initiative exceeded its objectives, with 133 businesses participating and 20,605 check-ins recorded. That year the program distributed $50,000 in Downtown Dollar Gift Cards, ensuring that the prize money stayed local. These created a 65% up-spend, which generated an additional $32,500 in economic activity by the end of 2024. The program has continued to expand its impact into 2025, reinforcing its role as a catalyst for both community vibrancy and economic resilience.

Downtowns across North America are still recovering from the impacts of the pandemic, compounded by public health and homelessness crises. Real progress is being made, but these improvements are not always visible or well understood by those outside these districts. To showcase the measurable, even transformational, changes happening in the central core of London, Ontario, the Downtown London BIA created the [Downtown Momentum Report](https://www.downtownlondon.ca/about-downtown-london-bia/research-and-reports/). Produced in collaboration with City of London staff and informed by data from Environics and the BIA itself, the report communicates to the BIA’s 1,400+ member businesses the progress that has been made and confirms the City’s commitment to revitalizing the downtown, outlining coordinated strategies for investments and programs in five areas: Economy, Vibrancy, Inclusion, Resilience, and Identity. The Momentum Report also serves to recognize the City of London and other partners for their support and investments, provides media with credible data to share downtown stories, encourages investors to build on the momentum of downtown projects, and offers valuable information for students studying urban issues. Ultimately, the report helps shape a more accurate and positive narrative, reinforcing why continued investment in a healthy and vibrant core is essential. report helps shape a more accurate and positive narrative, reinforcing why continued investment in a healthy and vibrant core is essential.

Shifting consumer habits, reduced foot traffic, and tariffs have made it harder for local businesses to compete with global online retailers. To help redirect spending back into local economies, Miconex Canada introduced the [Downtown Gift Card program](https://mi-cnx.com/canada-gift-cards), a simple but effective tool that encourages residents and visitors to shop locally. These “closed-loop” cards can only be redeemed at participating businesses within a defined district, ensuring that every dollar stays in the community. The program is now active in more than 42 Canadian towns and regions – from Grande Prairie to P.E.I. – and over $15 million in Downtown Gift Cards have been sold to date, supporting independent retailers, restaurants, and service providers of all sizes. Miconex works alongside BIAs, chambers of commerce, municipalities, and local sponsors to launch branded programs tailored to each district, using robust reporting tools to demonstrate measurable impact. These in turn attract additional support from corporate and government partners, who see the cards as a way to strengthen community ties and drive local growth. By turning strong consumer demand for shopping locally into direct economic results, Miconex is helping downtowns across Canada prosper and thrive in the face of ongoing change.

The [Downtown Vancouver Economic Dashboard](https://www.dtvan.ca/economic-dashboard/) is a publicly accessible online tool that illustrates the economic performance, activity, and overall health of the city’s downtown district. Featuring proprietary data and curated insights from the city’s Economic Development team, it provides regularly updated information on key indicators such as annual visits, storefront vacancy rates, and retail spending to track the shifting patterns in leasing, retail, transit, and visitor activity over time. While healthy downtown districts are an essential part of vibrant cities, there is often a lack of timely, accessible data that can inform city leaders and community members alike about their status. Downtown Van, a BIA, launched the dashboard to address this need, consolidating previously fragmented economic analysis into a holistic picture. It has recently been used to measure the success of downtown pilot programs such as the summer pedestrianization of the Gastown district. More importantly, Downtown Van’s leadership in community data has informed broader conversations on how governments can support other BIAs across British Columbia to access similar insights, with partnerships underway with the Canadian Urban Institute (CUI) and the Business Improvement Areas of British Columbia (BIABC) to help further democratize community data.olumbia to access similar insights, with partnerships underway with the Canadian Urban Institute (CUI) and the Business Improvement Areas of British Columbia (BIABC) to help further democratize community data.
Cash Coupons and Main Street Restoration Contest

Main Street Unionville, one of Markham’s best-loved destinations, has been undergoing a much-needed restoration. With construction scheduled during the summer – the busiest season for local businesses – there was a risk of reduced foot traffic and lost revenue. To help businesses retain customer traffic, the Main Street Unionville BIA launched a pair of creative marketing and support programs in partnership with the City of Markham, Destination Markham, local hotels, and the Markham Board of Trade. Phase 1 (April–May 2025) was the Main Street Cash Coupons program, in which 8,000 coupons redeemable at about 20 local businesses were distributed across Markham. This initiative generated an estimated $65,000 in economic impact and attracted more than 25,000 visitors, 60% of whom were first-time or infrequent patrons. Phase 2 (June–November 2025) featured the [Main Street Restoration Contest](https://unionville.ca/main-street-restoration-contest/), encouraging shopping at Unionville BIA businesses through receipt-based entries. The contest incentivized local shopping with total prizes of over $20,000 in $100 and $50 gift cards redeemable at participating businesses. These initiatives helped boost foot traffic and strengthen business confidence, demonstrating how Main Street districts can remain vibrant even through a major disruption.

Marketing is a persistent struggle for Main Street businesses and BIAs across Canada. Restricted budgets, limited in-house capacity, and the absence of the high-profile loyalty programs available at chain stores can reduce the direct engagement that builds a long-term customer base. To help overcome these barriers, marketing consultancy [ShopLocal2Win](https://www.shoplocal2win.com/) (SL2W) launched TapCanadian2Win, a six-week national “shop local/choose debit” contest, in late 2025. Customers who submitted receipts of $15 or more from a local business were entered into weekly $5,000 draws; debit users were eligible for an additional $5,000 bonus, incentivizing payments with lower transaction costs for retailers than credit cards. The owner of the shop that generated each winning receipt also received a cash prize. SL2W has successfully implemented similar campaigns for local BIAs, but with TapCanadian2Win backed by Interac as a national sponsor, the program’s larger scale reduces marketing costs for BIAs by 75% and eliminates the burden of finding local sponsors. The initiative is expected to generate $20 million nationwide in measurable economic impact by encouraging more frequent local purchases and lowering transaction costs for small businesses. The SL2W platform can provide reports on key performance indicators and return on investment, giving BIAs transparent data to demonstrate the program’s impact. TapCanadian2Win has the potential to be a powerful model for driving consumer loyalty, reinforcing business confidence, and ensuring the long-term vitality of Main Streets.

The lack of access to equitable and accessible support for entrepreneurs is an ongoing challenge in the City of Mississauga. [IDEA Mississauga](https://www.ideamississauga.ca/) is a City-led initiative that helps fill this gap by supporting entrepreneurs at all stages of their careers through a collaborative approach with local partners. In 2023, the project saw the opening of IDEA Square One, an entrepreneur support centre located in Ontario’s largest mall. It has expanded awareness and engagement with the initiative through targeted outreach, and now supports over 1,000 small businesses and startups annually. With a focus on inclusion, IDEA partners with YSpace (York University’s entrepreneurship and innovation hub), University of Toronto Mississauga, Sheridan College, the Black Entrepreneurship Alliance, Altitude Accelerator, and Canada’s Queer Chamber of Commerce to deliver culturally relevant programs and mentorship. Flagship initiatives like EmpowHER and Step-Up, which prioritize underrepresented founders, have doubled in size. In its first two years, IDEA Square One has provided over 500 consultations, helped launch 100 businesses, and raised over $12 million in funding for ventures supported by the program. With 80% of participants identifying as equity-deserving, IDEA fosters a trusted, community-driven ecosystem for inclusive growth. equity-deserving, IDEA fosters a trusted, community-driven ecosystem for inclusive growth.

In the fast-growing town of Caledon, Ontario – a community defined by both expansive rural geography and rapid development – supporting local businesses and entrepreneurs has been a unique challenge, and a centralized business support hub was long overdue. In 2024, the Town of Caledon launched the [Humber River Centre](https://www.caledonbusiness.ca/en/business-support/humber-river-centre.aspx) (HRC), transforming a former fire hall in downtown Bolton into an award winning, sustainable facility offering business support, coworking spaces, and economic development services. The HRC convenes key partners, including local business associations and regional innovation centres, to deliver coordinated programming and tailored support for entrepreneurs. To further strengthen early-stage business support, Caledon partnered with Toronto Metropolitan University’s tech incubator, [DMZ](https://dmz.torontomu.ca/), to pilot a three-year program that provides guidance on market readiness, access to funding, and mentorship – with a strong emphasis on equity and inclusion. Recognized by the [International Economic Development Council](https://www.iedconline.org/) for leadership in local economic growth, the HRC is proving that rural and mid-sized communities can deliver big-city innovation – and build resilient, thriving economies from the ground up.

Small tourism operators often face barriers to launching or growing their ideas due to limited access to funding, mentorship, and strategic support – challenges heightened by the sector’s dependence on seasonal trends and regional economic conditions. Hackforge, a non-profit organization that fosters innovation and entrepreneurship, aims to address these issues through the [Spark Program](https://www.tourisminnovation.ca/), part of its Tourism Innovation Lab. The program supports early-stage tourism entrepreneurs and community-driven ideas that promote a more accessible, inclusive, and sustainable tourism ecosystem in Canada. Each round of the program, which is delivered in Ontario and British Columbia, focuses on a specific theme or target group and is customized in partnership with municipalities, tourism organizations, provincial ministries, Regional Innovation Centres, the Canadian Queer Chamber of Commerce, and financial institutions. Applicants – from new business owners to individuals with untested ideas – complete a simple intake process, with shortlisted candidates invited to pitch to a panel of judges. Winners receive a $3,000 to $5,000 micro-grant and mentorship over three months to refine their ideas, build networks, and gain confidence, with some receiving additional support such as website development. By empowering local entrepreneurs to transform creative ideas into viable ventures, “Spark” helps strengthen regional economies and ensures the tourism sector remains innovative and inclusive.
Toronto and Ottawa, ON & Vancouver, BC & Calgary, AB

STACKT Market in Toronto is the largest shipping container market in North America. It has become a shared space for small businesses, global brands, and community events, one that also supports the local economy. Building on this model, STACKT launched [STACKTˣ](https://stacktx.com/) in 2023, a national platform designed to help small businesses launch and grow. At its core, STACKTˣ is an eight-week accelerator program that offers entrepreneurs mentorship, marketing, and operations support along with a one-month free retail lease in a high-foot-traffic area in its modular market space. Operating in Toronto and Ottawa, with expansions planned for Calgary, Vancouver, and beyond, STACKTˣ has already attracted over 7,500 small businesses and 1,600 Storefront Grant applicants, enabling 30 recipients to open pop-up shops. By providing real-world exposure, expert guidance, and accessible retail opportunities, STACKTˣ fills a gap in Canada’s entrepreneurial ecosystem. Programs like this not only help emerging businesses thrive but also generate local jobs, activate communities, and strengthen urban resilience. STACKTˣ shows how place-based innovation can translate into national impact – empowering entrepreneurs while redefining how cities grow, collaborate, and sustain economic vitality.

Many of the City of Regina’s most beloved local businesses operate in former single-family homes that were converted over time. However, bringing these properties up to modern building codes can be costly and complex, particularly for small business owners managing limited budgets and tight timelines. Recognizing that these challenges were discouraging investment and leaving some buildings vacant, the City invested in research and analysis to make conversions more predictable and affordable. Municipal staff developed a set of pre-approved, code-compliant alternatives to address common barriers faced by owners. The result is a [practical user guide](https://www.regina.ca/export/sites/Regina.ca/bylaws-permits-licences/building-demolition/.galleries/pdfs/Advisory-House-to-Commercial.pdf) that connects business owners to Service Coordinators, streamlines the approval process, and provides links to detailed engineering resources for professionals. Applicants for building conversions now benefit from dedicated regulatory support, clearer statements of construction scope, and access to City incentive programs that can offset costs. By establishing these accessible guidelines, the City has created a pathway that prioritizes local business vitality while preserving 60-to-100-year-old homes rich with character – a win for both Regina’s downtown and its residents.

In summer 2025, the [Stratford Perth Centre for Business](https://www.stratfordperthbusiness.ca/) piloted Caffeine and Commerce, a program that aims to create a casual, inclusive, and low-pressure environment for small business owners to connect. The program responds to a growing desire among young and diverse entrepreneurs in small cities for authentic, community-based connection points that recognize their experiences, challenges, and identities. Caffeine and Commerce addresses this need by offering an accessible alternative to traditional, formal networking events: biweekly meetups at rotating cafes across Stratford, Ontario, with no registration, formal agenda, or icebreakers – just a welcoming space to drop in, ask questions, share ideas, and make genuine connections over coffee. Organizers compiled recurring questions and collected wisdom from these sessions into short, shareable resources such as mini-guides, reels, and live Q&As. While the initiative began as a summer pilot, its small-scale, human-centred approach to business support has the potential to be formalized into a year-round program with backing from municipal, tourism, and innovation partners, and to be adapted in other communities.

Local economic development and business support organization [LOCO BC](https://www.locobc.ca/cpages/commercialaffordability) is tackling a growing issue facing independent businesses today: commercial affordability. By gathering and analyzing data from a wide range of stakeholders, including developers, property owners, leasing agents, property managers, and business and community associations, LOCO BC is aiming to discover what defines a strong tenant mix and how affordability can be measured and sustained over time. This province-wide initiative responds to the growing challenge of rising costs and unstable lease rates, which make it difficult for small, independent businesses to remain in their spaces over the long term. This results in high tenant turnover, neglected properties, and premature deterioration of buildings, which diminishes the overall quality of local commercial areas. With its commercial affordability initiative, LOCO BC is bridging gaps between small business owners and the development community, seeking to dispel the myth that local businesses are riskier tenants compared to larger, more established companies. The feedback received has been overwhelmingly positive, showcasing the importance of commercial affordability for small, local businesses to the long-term health of communities and local economies.

Toronto is home to over 160 public markets: farmers' markets, vintage and antique markets, artisan and craft markets, affordable fresh food markets, and more. The key role that such markets play in supporting local businesses and building strong, connected communities is often overlooked. Enter [marketcityTO](https://www.marketcityto.org/), led by a growing grassroots network of former market managers supporting Toronto’s public markets sector through collaborative projects and advocacy that help residents and municipal representatives recognize the value of public markets. Working with market managers, marketcityTO has led initiatives such as Toronto’s first [interactive market map](https://www.marketcityto.org/map), the Scarborough Fresh Food Pilot, and the 11th International Public Market Conference. Their engagement with councillors, City staff, and other stakeholders informed the City’s first-ever [Public Markets Action Plan](https://www.toronto.ca/business-economy/industry-sector-support/public-markets/public-markets-action-plan/) and led to a dedicated full-time staff position. In 2025, marketcityTO partnered with the City to expand Public Markets Week – a citywide celebration of the culture, diversity, and entrepreneurship that markets bring to Toronto’s neighbourhoods. A pilot program provided funding for markets to host programming as part of the event. Ten markets across Toronto collaborated with local organizations and small businesses on initiatives such as Indigenous-led medicine bag workshops, willow weaving, and cooking demonstrations. Leveraging Toronto’s Love Local campaign, marketcityTO continues to highlight that supporting public markets is one of the most effective ways to strengthen a municipality’s small business ecosystem and community connections.

Toronto’s mental health system had long been overstretched and underfunded, which has led to a growing need for reactive crisis response from emergency services, including police. Seeking an alternative approach, the City of Toronto launched the [Toronto Community Crisis Service](https://www.toronto.ca/community-people/public-safety-alerts/community-safety-wellbeing-programs/toronto-community-crisis-service/) (TCCS), which provides free, confidential, trauma-informed in-person support led by mental health workers instead of police. After a pilot in 2022, the TCCS expanded in 2024 to a service providing 24/7 crisis response to everyone age 16 and over, city-wide. TCCS is accessed through a non-police crisis line (2-1-1) or as a transfer from 9-1-1. Mobile crisis teams respond directly to calls with immediate support as well as offering follow-up care, including up to 90 days of case management. TCCS teams include community nurses, harm reduction workers, peers with lived experience, case managers, and Indigenous elders. This approach helps reduce the potential danger and trauma of mental health emergencies, particularly for Black, Indigenous, and 2SLGBTQ+ residents, who face serious risks and systemic biases during police interactions. TCCS has diverted more than 30,000 calls that would otherwise have gone to traditional emergency services, resolving almost 80% of calls transferred from 9-1-1 without police involvement. In November 2025, the service expanded to include a pilot program on the TTC. TCCS demonstrates that cities can prioritize care, dignity, and community leadership without relying on enforcement-based responses.

Despite being among those most in need of social services, unhoused people often face serious barriers to accessing support through traditional service pathways, including long waitlists, discontinuity of services, lack of trust in providers, and inconsistent access to phones. Toronto’s services have often been reactive, reaching people when they are already in crisis or facing severe health challenges. In addition, this population is often criminalized, which can create further barriers to their support and well-being. To better address this community’s needs, Toronto Public Health launched the [Downtown Community Outreach Response & Engagement Team](https://www.toronto.ca/community-people/health-wellness-care/health-programs-advice/downtown-community-outreach-response-engagement-team/) (CORE) in partnership with the Toronto Police Service in December 2024. CORE grew from the Downtown Yonge BIA's [Community Engagement Team](https://downtownyonge.com/community-engagement-team/) (CET), which started in 2018 with funding from Toronto’s BIA Innovation Fund to respond to people in crisis in streetfront businesses. CORE’s mandate is broader: a proactive outreach (not emergency-response) service, with teams of nurses and police officers who provide both immediate medical care and short-term case management from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily, anywhere in the Yonge-Dundas area of downtown. The teams coordinate access to mental health supports, primary care clinics, and basic living supplies like sleeping bags. It’s a model for proactively supporting people experiencing homelessness where they are, building trust and improving continuity of care.

Launched in August 2024, Ottawa’s [Alternate Neighbourhood Crisis Response](https://www.centretownchc.org/anchor) (ANCHOR) is a community-led program that provides a culturally sensitive and equity-centered response to mental health and substance use crises 24/7. Residents can access the service by calling 2-1-1, with multilingual support available in Arabic, Cantonese, Swahili, and Somali, reflecting Centretown’s diverse community. ANCHOR’s design is based on best practices and community recommendations from the research outlined in the 2023 report by the Ottawa Guiding Council on Mental Health and Addictions. In its first year, ANCHOR received 4,464 calls, with 92% of them resolved with no police involvement. ANCHOR is a key pillar of Ottawa’s 2021–2031 Community Safety and Well-Being Plan, implemented in collaboration with Community Navigation Eastern Ontario, Centretown Community Health Center (CHC) and Somerset West CHC. Implementation started in Centretown – a small, densely populated area with high need – allowing ANCHOR to measure its impact and refine its approach before expanding it services. This expansion is being implemented gradually, guided by community feedback, evaluation outcomes, and sustainable funding opportunities. ANCHOR is building a strong foundation for long-term system change, demonstrating the value of collaborative, community-led solutions to complex challenges.
Enabling housing through research and innovation

Transit-oriented development (TOD) has the potential to improve access to opportunity and incentivize sustainable growth, but transit developments across Canada have often led to speculation from rising land value, displacing vulnerable residents and making it difficult to sustain and build affordable and non-market housing. The [Canadian Alliance for Transit Connected Housing](https://sicanada.org/program/catch/) (CATCH) is a new approach to TOD that places affordability and inclusion at the centre. CATCH originated from a CMHC lab led by Social Innovation Canada in partnership with CMHC, the City of Hamilton, the Hamilton Community Foundation, non-market housing providers, and other stakeholders, who co-designed a solution that aligns transit investments with long-term affordability. It is anchored by the CATCH Fund – Canada’s first transit-oriented affordable housing fund. The CATCH Fund blends public and private capital, complemented by municipal grants, to provide flexible financing needed to preserve and create affordable housing near transit. The $18.7M fund is expected to launch in early 2026 with a pipeline of projects ready for investment. The Hamilton lab also influenced municipal policy, informing zoning changes, rental protections, and the city’s new Rental Housing Protection By-law to preserve existing stock and protect tenants. CATCH aims to scale this success nationally, develop a catalogue of best practices, convene local collaboratives, and apply proven social finance models.

[Balanced Supply of Housing](https://bsh.ubc.ca/) (BSH) is a collaborative network of academic researchers and community partners based at the University of British Columbia that conducts research to generate and mobilize knowledge for a more equitable housing system. BSH advances long-term affordable housing solutions by supporting community land trusts (CLTs) that remove land from speculative markets and place it under community control. Partnering with CLTs across Canada, BSH funds research, policy development, and land acquisitions that protect affordability, prevent displacement, and promote equity – especially for marginalized communities. Evidence from BSH-supported studies, such as the Parkdale Tower Rental Housing Study in Toronto’s west end, has informed public acquisition programs and enabled the successful preservation and creation of affordable housing, demonstrating that CLTs are a viable and effective tool in addressing the housing crisis. Through more than forty projects focused on innovative land practices and alternatives to the financialization of housing, BSH builds the capacity of community-led housing initiatives. Projects include policy reports, a profile series on Canadian CLTs, and community capacity-building initiatives to enhance the delivery of affordable housing. This important work highlights the power of CLTs to transform housing from a commodity to a shared community asset.

[Homeway Benefits](https://www.homewaybenefits.com/home) is a British Columbia-based company that is redefining workforce benefits by making a path toward homeownership a standard part of employee packages. As home ownership rates continue to decline and younger Canadians have fewer pathways to buy homes, Homeway partners with employers to help employees build financial stability through an innovative savings model. In this program, 5–10% of each employee’s paycheque is matched by the employer and invested into a fund, allowing employees to accumulate between $15,000 and $30,000 toward a downpayment over a three- to four-year term. Partnered with the North Peace Community Foundation to manage the fund, Homeway Benefits piloted the model with the Fort St. John Association for Community Living (FSJACL) and is now working to expand it more broadly. While this program was designed for rural and northern communities, the concept is adaptable for urban centres; Homeway Benefits is currently in communication with Key, a company offering 2.5%-downpayment mortgages in Toronto and Vancouver, to explore potential collaboration. By turning the dream of homeownership into a shared journey between employers and employees, Homeway Benefits helps individuals build lasting equity and stability, while their employers benefit from improved retention and loyalty.

As Toronto makes strides toward building affordable housing, some of the barriers to more rapid progress are related to information access: siloed data, inconsistent intergovernmental coordination, and highly technical language that makes it difficult for residents to understand or engage with development process. Seeing this as a problem that civic tech could address, housing advocates launched HousingNowTO in December 2018 as a volunteer-run, open-source platform to bridge the gap between housing professionals and the public. By translating complex data into clear, accessible information through Google maps, photographs, videos, and data visualization, [HousingNowTO](https://www.google.com/maps/d/u/0/viewer?mid=1ROhMQUHXmVMyeyXJcHT7eSuVLiSnwFQN&ll=43.70402728923885%2C-79.40693935&z=12) equips residents with the tools to understand and evaluate affordable housing projects on government-owned lands. Its mapping portal and social media channels function as a framework for public transparency and accountability, offering data-driven viability analysis of proposed sites and reducing misinformation. The platform has delivered tangible results, including adding thousands of additional rental units to the City’s original redevelopment plans. The organization is also expanding the community of housing supporters by mentoring over a hundred university students in housing data advocacy. Recognized as a finalist in the 2024 World Smart Cities Awards, HousingNowTO shows how open-government and civic-tech models can be scaled to empower communities and strengthen public accountability in housing delivery.

At time when rural Canada has its own housing crisis, [Innovation Building Group](https://innovationbuilding.com/) (IBG) has pioneered a new approach that delivers affordable, high-performance, climate-resilient family homes. IBG’s approach combines modular construction with advanced building technologies to create durable, “energy-ready” homes – that is, homes designed and built to be adaptable to evolving energy standards without costly retrofits, reducing long-term costs and environmental impact. By integrating hydronic heat pumps, non-load-bearing composite cladding, insulated concrete-form foundations, and energy-recovery ventilators, IBG has reduced both construction and operating costs for homes that can sustain comfortable temperatures in the Canadian climate. These homes eliminate reliance on natural gas, using airtight envelopes and high-performance windows to boost resilience and energy efficiency. This model is designed for replication across Canada’s smaller towns, offering Canadian Home Builders’ Association builders a practical path to transition from traditional single-family homes to compact, community-oriented developments. The Oso project in Golden, B.C. – an award-winning net-zero energy-ready hub – demonstrates IBG’s commitment to revitalizing rural centers through sustainable design. IBG is shaping the future of Canada’s missing-middle housing with purpose-built solutions that serve both people and the planet.
Modular row housing on vacant land

Many cities have some amount of vacant and underused land: largely empty parking lots, remnants of low-density sprawl, abandoned properties that haven’t been taken up by new owners, and so on. In British Columbia, the [Rapid Housing Foundation](https://www.rapidhousing.ca/) (RHF) is working to turn over an estimated 84,000 vacant and viable parcels into modular row housing for seniors and low-income residents. RHF plans to install factory-built units in under four months by using temporary foundations. On the financing side, the plan is to lease residential lots rather than purchase land, and to make units that qualify for British Columbia’s shelter-rate assistance. The rental revenue guaranteed from British Columbia’s rent subsidies, combined with RHF's low per-unit costs (about $100,000), eliminate the need for government capital grants by making it easier to secure private financing from funders like BMO, Vancity, and RBC, so each development will be financially viable. While RHF will have to find alternatives for British Columbia’s rent subsidies when it expands to other provinces, its model for quickly and cheaply building housing on existing vacant land can be adopted throughout the country.

Founded to tackle Canada’s housing crisis – particularly the “missing middle” of infill mid-rise and affordable housing – [Assembly Corp](https://assemblycorp.ca/) is transforming how housing gets built in Canada through mass timber panelized construction. Traditional construction methods are often slow, costly, and unpredictable, making it difficult for governments, non-profits, and developers to deliver accessible homes at the pace and scale required. Assembly Corp’s approach is to treat buildings like products. They design standardized, modular mass timber and light-frame wood panels, manufacture them off-site, and assemble them on-site. This sustainable, modular approach cuts project timelines in half, reduces carbon emissions by up to 60%, and brings predictability to a process long defined by delays and overruns. By leveraging renewable Canadian wood, Assembly Corp ensures high-quality, low-waste construction while exceeding energy code requirements by 20% – and also enhancing resident well-being through nature-based design. With a focus on human-scale density and low-carbon communities, Assembly Corp is proving that building faster can also mean building smarter, greener, and more inclusively.

In addition to improving construction efficiency and sustainability, [modular solutions](https://nowhousing.com/) can also address urgent social needs by delivering supportive housing and site services for people with nowhere else to go. The “sleep cabin community” is a supportive housing model that creates clusters of 20 to 50 furnished cabins surrounding a central community centre offering 24/7 staff support and wraparound services. In Waterloo, The Working Centre operates a 50-cabin site equipped with electricity, heating, and cooling, providing mental health and addiction supports, as well as helping residents transition to permanent housing. In Peterborough, the Elizabeth Fry Society manages a similar 50-unit Modular Bridge Housing Community as part of the city’s Interim Housing Solutions strategy, connecting residents to supports and long-term housing. Since 2019, about 140 cabins have been installed across Ontario, helping to reduce homelessness and save lives. Although these projects often face initial community resistance, many neighbours ultimately become advocates – volunteering and supporting the initiative, demonstrating how cabin communities embody compassion and possibility.

Located in London, Ontario, in the historic Victoria Hospital Lands neighbourhood, [Village Soho](https://www.villagesoho.ca/) brings together six non-profit housing developers to create nearly 700 mixed-income apartments, with over 30% designed to be barrier-free. The initiative is a response to the deepening housing crisis in the city, where over 2,000 residents face homelessness and 7,200 wait for subsidized housing. Convened by the London Community Foundation, Village SoHo brings six non-profit housing developers together to address the issue, aiming to create a place that fosters strong, safe and accessible community while celebrating the neighbourhood's rich history. [Indwell](https://indwell.ca/soho) is a founding member of the Village SoHo Alliance, which will restore two heritage buildings on site to create 138 new apartments. These restorations preserve architectural legacy while offering modern, affordable homes with wraparound supports. Construction began in fall 2023, with full completion expected by summer 2028. This collaborative model demonstrates how non-profit leadership, municipal support, and community fundraising can transform underused land into inclusive, sustainable housing.

Based in the Greater Toronto Area, [Reena](https://reena.org/)’s intentional community housing model reimagines housing as a foundation for dignity, autonomy, health, and social inclusion by integrating care, accessibility, and community under one roof. Through three purpose-built residences – the Sandy Keshen Reena Residence (2012), Lou Fruitman Reena Residence (2021), and upcoming Frankfort Family Reena Residence (2026) – Reena provides homes for seniors and for individuals with developmental disabilities and physical and mental health challenges. Each residence provides essential services such as medical care, mental health supports, life-skills training, and personal care, enabling residents to live independently within inclusive, mixed communities rather than segregated facilities. This model has potential to help alleviate Ontario’s long-standing shortage of supportive housing – over 40,000 individuals are on waitlists, with the result that many people who would do well in supportive housing are institutionalized, unnecessarily hospitalized, or homeless. Developed in partnership with Ontario Health and a number of organizations such as March of Dimes and Safehaven, the model brings multiple care providers together as a single multidisciplinary team. By uniting housing and health-care systems that have long operated in silos, Reena’s model delivers co-ordinated, cost-effective support that is 10 to 13 times less expensive per day than institutional care. Building on this success, Reena currently chairs the Intentional Community Consortium (ICC), which works to solve the housing crisis for those with developmental disabilities.

A shortage of accessible housing, particularly residential homes suitable for people with mobility challenges, severely limits the rental and homeownership options of many individuals with accessibility needs. The [No Limits Collective](https://www.nolimitscollective.com/) (NLC) incentivizes homeowners and small investors to build accessible rental or investment properties, offering free property management services – including tenant placement and issue resolution – for homes that meet a basic accessibility standard. Red Plain Developments, NLC’s licensed development subsidiary, exclusively builds barrier-free homes while also pushing municipal bylaws and construction technologies to increase the value and investment potential of accessible housing. NLC is endorsed by Spinal Cord Injury Alberta (SCI) and Voices of Albertans with Disabilities (VAD), and both these organizations serve as NLC’s tenant placement partners, matching available homes with the residents who need them most. Homes built through the program are listed in a private online directory accessible only to trusted partners, ensuring efficient placement and relieving pressure on public and communal facilities. The approach is scalable across communities, and the program empowers vetted “No Limits Builders” to offer the program to their clients, expanding access to barrier-free homes and generating meaningful community impact.

Extreme heat events pose serious health risks, particularly for vulnerable populations who have limited access to safe drinking water. During the City of Edmonton’s community engagement on its extreme weather policy – which addresses risks from poor air quality, extreme cold, and extreme heat – dehydration was identified as the primary health concern. In response, the city launched a pilot project in 2021, [equipping five fire hydrants with attachments that function as public water fountains](https://www.edmonton.ca/programs_services/emergency_preparedness/extreme-weather-summer), allowing people to refill bottles and ensuring accessible, safe hydration during the hottest months. Community demand was strong during the pilot, and, given its relatively low cost, the program was expanded. By summer 2023, the number of stations across Edmonton had grown to 30, all operating 24/7 from May through September. (To enhance accessibility, the city developed an [online map](https://www.edmonton.ca/programs_services/emergency_preparedness/extreme-weather-summer) of water station locations.) This initiative provides a critical lifeline for residents during prolonged heat waves, reducing the risk of dehydration and related illnesses. It provides an excellent example of a simple, scalable program that municipalities can implement to protect public health and increase equity in the face of rising extreme climate events.

Wildfire smoke can travel thousands of kilometres, exposing even populations that are a great distance away to poor air quality. In June 2023, Toronto experienced its first major episode of wildfire smoke, prompting the city government to recognize the need for a coordinated local response. In turn, Toronto Public Health developed its first Wildfire Smoke Response Strategy, outlining seasonal updates, strategies for response, and preparedness activities. A key component of this strategy is the Cleaner Air Spaces (CAS) network, introduced in 2024 to provide safe, accessible spaces for residents during smoke events. Six City facilities were designated as CAS sites. Each location is equipped with high-efficiency MERV-13 air filtration systems to reduce fine particulate matter from wildfire smoke. These spaces are available to the public during their regular operating hours, offering short-term relief for residents, particularly those without access to effective ventilation or air filtration at home. The CAS initiative is currently a pilot; Toronto Public Health is implementing air quality monitoring to evaluate effectiveness and guide improvements. But it has the potential to contribute positively to the health and well-being of Toronto residents over the long term.

In April 2023, the city council of Richmond, B.C., endorsed the Richmond [Circular City Strategy](https://www.richmond.ca/circulareconomy), an ambitious plan with a vision for the city to achieve 100% circularity by 2050. The circular economy model moves beyond the predominant linear take-make-use-dispose economic model – which leads to the overuse of virgin materials and environmental issues like soil contamination – and embraces closing resource loops to combine economic growth with sustainable practices. Richmond is the first city in North America to adopt this framework, which aligns with the sustainability goals in the city’s Official Community Plan. The strategy, which can be aligned with upcoming federal and provincial programs and regulatory mandates, has six areas of focus: Maximizing Ecosystem Services, Regenerative Food System, Resilient and Innovative Economy, Shared Mobility, Adaptive Built Environment, and Products and Materials Management. It calls for extensive community and industry consultation, which encourages innovation through experimentation and learning by doing, thus supporting the development of new business models and sustainable practices. This inclusive approach also ensures that residents' needs remain central, enhancing community engagement and participation. Envisioned as a flexible blueprint rather than a fixed work, the Richmond Circular City Strategy is an example of cities taking the lead in sustainable urban planning by embedding circular economy principles into their plans and practices to reimagine how resources can flow in a sustainable, equitable, low-carbon economy.

It takes a lot of small repairs to keep sustainable urban transportation infrastructure – such as bike lanes, pedestrian crossings, and public transit vehicles – running smoothly throughout the city. Operations and maintenance departments are responsible for managing numerous small, widespread, and persistent issues, such as potholes, broken bikeway curbs, malfunctioning crosswalk buttons, and blocked curb cuts. While minor, these problems have a significant impact on residents’ day-to-day travel, yet are often overlooked in capital planning cycles. Unfixed disruptions undermine safety, accessibility, and public trust, especially for those who rely on walking, biking, and/or public transit to get around, creating cascading effects for mobility and equity. The City of Toronto is working creatively to address this persistent operational challenge, finding new ways effectively and equitably deliver on small-scale repairs that are too often delayed or deprioritized. City staff are piloting alternative procurement models suitable for small but high-impact transportation maintenance tasks. One element includes developing flexible, on-call contracts with approved vendors for small jobs, eliminating the need for lengthy and competitive procurement processes. The goal is to create a replicable approach that other cities can adopt to deliver more efficient public-realm improvements that help keep people moving in a sustainable way and enhance public trust in core city services.

Seeing a need for visual data tools about health and climate readiness that are geared toward non-technical audiences, NatuR&D spearheaded the [Resilient Urban Systems & Habitat (RUSH) Initiative](https://whatstherush.ca/). Based on Southern Vancouver Island and hosted in partnership with Peninsula Streams & Shorelines and the Map Shop at the University of Victoria, RUSH integrates climate data, citizen science, and Indigenous knowledge into an accessible GIS platform. The project is a collaborative, open-access effort aimed at enhancing ecological resilience and community well-being through participatory mapping that increases local knowledge of nature-based solutions. The interactive maps cover a wide range of subjects, from local climate-readiness initiatives like rain gardens to sources of farm-fresh produce to neighbourhood factors that contribute to long-term health and happiness, such as parks. The initiative combines research with practical opportunities to get involved, for example by creating a rain garden or taking the bus from a nearby stop. Linking hyperlocal information with everyday action and the chance to contribute, the project connects people more closely with the natural environment and encourages a sense of belonging. By fostering public awareness and data-driven decision-making, as well as supporting local reconciliation through Indigenous partnerships, RUSH empowers communities to address environmental challenges collaboratively.

Since 2009, [Green Neighbours 21](https://gn21.ca/) (GN21) has brought together a network of community members to advise each other about energy resilience and residential retrofits. Located in the St. Paul’s neighbourhood of Toronto, GN21 assembles program delivery partners to train interested volunteers, build an informed and engaged community, and share personal stories as models for “going green.” Through regular meetings and a series of online fact sheets, the program helps neighbours advise neighbours on everything from energy efficiency upgrades and building envelopes to cisterns and backflow valves to native species planting. The group also partners with Transition Toronto to host an annual EcoFair, the largest sustainability event of its kind in the city, which draws over 1,200 attendees and dozens of non-profits to share information about environmentally friendly actions. In creating a place where neighbours can learn from and help each other, GN21 is creating new connections and points of trust while building local resilience.

Assessing embodied carbon impacts throughout a building’s life cycle is an essential step in advancing regenerative and low-carbon design. As a sector, buildings are the third-largest greenhouse gas emitters Canada, yet many professionals in the architecture, engineering, and construction sector lack access to the tools and training needed to assess and reduce building emissions. The practice of life cycle assessment (LCA) provides a framework for evaluating a building’s environmental footprint – from material extraction to operations and through end of life – but remains underused due to limited awareness and training opportunities, especially outside major urban centres. To address this gap, the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada (RAIC), in partnership with the National Research Council of Canada, launched a rapid-deployment national initiative to build LCA capacity across the sector. The bilingual program includes instructor-led [workshops](https://raic.org/LCAworkshop) held across nine regions, with an on-demand module launched in summer 2025. These workshops, presented in collaboration with Ha/f Climate Design, combine theory with hands-on case studies. To date, the initiative has equipped over 1,500 participants – small firms, large practices, public agencies, and Indigenous communities – with practical skills to assess embodied carbon and integrate LCA into building design, procurement, and policy. By equipping a community of professionals with the knowledge they need to incorporate LCA into their work, the RAIC is advancing the transition to low-carbon built environments in Canada.
Peel Region,York Region, and Toronto, ON

Many organizations want to transition to more sustainable practices but lack the resources and knowledge to do so. Since 2008, [Partners in Project Green](https://partnersinprojectgreen.com/) (PPG) has been helping to build this capacity in businesses, government organizations, academic institutions, and utilities across the Greater Toronto Area through workshops, peer learning, and collaborative initiatives to make organizations more sustainable. A strategic collaboration between the TRCA and Toronto’s Pearson Airport, PPG focuses on four key areas: energy performance, waste management, water stewardship, and employee engagement. Over the past 15 years, the initiative has diverted nearly 20,000 tonnes of waste from landfills and saved the emissions equivalent of 58,000 round-trip flights from Toronto to Vancouver, among other impacts. What stands out about PPG is that it is led by businesses themselves, with TRCA providing guidance and a platform. Structured on a membership funding-based model, PPG translates high-level climate goals into localized action, helping organizations share knowledge to promote climate resilience at every level from individual organizations to whole regions. By equipping businesses with tools, partnerships, and knowledge, PPG demonstrates that economic growth and environmental leadership can work together to build a more sustainable future.

TransformTO, the City of Toronto’s Net Zero Strategy, has an ambitious goal of increasing the number of people who travel by cycling, walking, or public transit to 75% of all trips under five kilometres by 2030. This achievement would increase the number of cyclists in the city significantly – and [Bike Training Collective Canada](https://tcat.ca/project/bike-training-collective-canada/) is already planning how to support them. Today, there are about 200 bike mechanics working in Toronto who service 53,000 bikes every year, but by 2030, the city will need many more to maintain its growing fleet – between 3,000 and 12,400. The collective spent two years identifying training organizations and promoting bike mechanic training, and in 2024 began a process of securing the necessary funding to implement its training program. This phase also included employer engagement to help newly graduated bike mechanics find jobs. The initiative has already added nearly 20% more bike mechanics to the industry – a significant change in a short time. In addition to support from industry partners, the program has secured funding from the Centre for Active Transportation, the City of Toronto, The Learning Enrichment Foundation, CultureLink, Charlie's Freewheels, The Canadian E-Bike Association, and the Peter Gilgan Foundation. By anticipating future needs, Bike Training Collective Canada is supporting both economic growth today and a more active city in the future.

The Town of Golden, B.C. has adapted Columbia Basin Trust’s [Resident Directed (ReDi) Grants](https://www.golden.ca/town-hall/town-council/resident-directed-redi-grants-program) program to provide sustained support for projects that address local priorities and broadly benefit the community. Grants typically range from $5,000 to $100,000 and have been awarded to a diverse range of organizations across the region. With funding provided in partnership with Columbia Basin Trust, Golden’s ReDi Grants model follows an iterative “Plan–Do–Check–Act” approach. The process begins with the community identifying local priorities, guided by the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and reflected in the Golden & District Community Foundation’s annual Vital Pulse Survey. Non-profit organizations then develop project proposals that align with these priorities. An adjudication committee reviews applications and selects projects that best reflect community needs and desired outcomes. Upon completion, project leaders report back on their results and contributions toward SDG targets. This “full-circle” approach integrates local data, citizen education, feedback, and rubric refinement to strengthen accountability and improve project effectiveness. Over time, the process enhances local funders’ ability to communicate progress, listen to residents, support organizations, and report to stakeholders, engaging a broader cross-section of the community and fostering continuous improvement through each funding cycle.

The [Mini Forest program](https://greencommunitiescanada.org/programs/mini-forest/), launched in 2023 by Green Communities Canada and its partners, is a growing initiative that brings community-driven forest planting to urban areas across the country. The program supports municipalities and local organizations to transform under-natured spaces into dense, biodiverse forests. Mini forests – also known as micro-forests, tiny forests, or, after the Japanese botanist who popularized them, as Miyawaki forests – are compact ecosystems of native trees and shrubs planted closely together in multilayered arrangements that mimic natural forests. The method emphasizes careful soil preparation and diversity in species selection, resulting in accelerated tree growth and a thriving habitat for pollinators and wildlife. Beyond ecological benefits, mini forests have many positive effects such as improving air quality, cooling urban heat islands, reducing stormwater flooding, and creating restorative green spaces that support mental health and community connection. The Mini Forests program provides training, tools, and resources to design, plant, and maintain mini forests, and offers capacity-building workshops and research partnerships to monitor long-term outcomes. From 2023 through 2025, the initiative planted 46 mini forests across Canada, engaging over 3,500 volunteers to install them in spaces such as parks, colleges, and community centres.

Cities are experiencing the impacts of climate change more acutely than other areas because of the urban heat island effect: paved and built surfaces can reach temperatures 27–50°C hotter than the surrounding air. To help municipalities plan for and mitigate the effects of extreme heat, Evergreen developed [AI for the Resilient City](https://www.evergreen.ca/impacts/ai-for-the-resilient-city/), a data visualization and analytics tool that identifies areas most affected by urban heat using public and proprietary data combined with machine learning. Supported in part by the RBC Foundation through RBC Tech for Nature, the tool helps cities shape evidence-based policies on green space and urban forests. Its features allow municipalities to simulate future changes, test interventions, and compare environmental, socio-economic, and infrastructure data across time. Built in collaboration with Gramener, it enables users to visualize and model at a hyperlocal scale to show how built and natural environments influence local heat conditions. The program has so far worked with the City of Calgary, Halifax Regional Municipality, and Peel Region, along with the Toronto and Region Conservation Authority, and continues to expand. By showing not just where cities are vulnerable, but where they can make strategic interventions, the tool empowers communities to make informed planning and infrastructure decisions, strengthening urban resilience in a rapidly warming climate.

The field of sustainability measurement and reporting has to date largely focused on assessing how impacts are changing relative to past performance or competitors. Today, municipalities are increasingly transitioning from incrementally doing less harm to aligning with the science- and ethics based thresholds that define sustainability. These thresholds represent the quantifiable limits of our ecological systems and the basic human needs that are critical to our well-being. The UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the [Doughnut Economics model](https://doughnuteconomics.org/doughnut/) have popularized thresholds-based goals at a macro scale, but further progress depends on being able to downscale them for communities and organizations. To address the lack of useful guidance available, the [Flourishing Enterprise Institute](https://flourishingenterpriseinstitute.org/) has been working with a collective of partners to further develop and mobilize the Context-Based Sustainability (CBS) accounting method, founded by the Centre for Sustainable Organizations in 2005. CBS is the world’s first thresholds-based and equity-informed management accounting method. Successful applications include the City of Nanaimo, which adopted “The Doughnut” but struggled to define authentic thresholds at a local scale. In 2021, the city became the first municipality in the world to adopt CBS, which enabled it to develop a set of thresholds-based indicators and metrics tailored to its unique local context. The results have enhanced performance management and strategic decision-making, and have been widely recognized as a leading example within the municipal sector.

Extreme heat can make life very uncomfortable in cities. There are strategies that can mitigate this effect, but incorporating them into urban design is a complicated process for which most cities lack the tools. To help urban planners and city staff create and assess designs for thermal comfort, a team of environmental building engineers created [CityDigitalTwin](https://www.greenleaves.app/) (CDT), an advanced urban-scale simulation platform for evaluating the outdoor thermal comfort, microclimate, and environmental impacts of urban design. The tool simulates large and complex urban regions, allowing for scenario testing and climate adaptation planning at the local scale. The tool, designed for non-expert users, has a graphical interface that allows users to import city geometry, define materials and vegetation, and run simulations to assess the effects of design alternatives on thermal comfort, wind, radiation, and surface temperatures. CDT has been used in Toronto to identify strategies for mitigating the urban heat-island effect, in New York City to understand the impact of new high-rise construction on urban vegetation performance, and in Singapore to assess the environmental implications of building a new sports stadium. With its ability to focus at the scale of buildings, neighbourhoods, and cities, CDT can help municipalities mitigate the risks of extreme heat, increasing the comfort of their residents and providing more equitable health outcomes.

In Toronto’s Niagara neighbourhood, two siblings created an edible children’s garden to bring greenery, joy, and connection to their community. Motivated by the lack of child-friendly areas nearby, they envisioned a space where area children could gather, play, and learn about nature. With support from their condo corporation, they transformed a modest plot of dirt near the condo into a vibrant, edible oasis. Now in its third year, the garden features native plants and seasonal vegetables, inviting children to explore, taste, and tend to the land. It has become a hub of activity: kids ride bikes, play soccer in the laneway, and build friendships rooted in shared care for the space. This volunteer-led initiative is powered by community donations and a spirit of collaboration. Its goals remain simple but powerful: create a welcoming spot for children, foster a stronger sense of community, and spread happiness through nature. The garden is more than a patch of green – it’s a living example of how small, local efforts can reshape urban life for the better.

The hyperlocal publication [The Green Line](https://thegreenline.to/) uses a unique “action journey” model to transform how young Torontonians engage with democracy – through culture and community-led storytelling. In a time when young people are facing rising anxiety, disillusionment, and civic disengagement, this month-long media model offers a hopeful alternative: journalism that doesn’t just inform but mobilizes people to take action. Each action journey guides participants through four phases: explaining systemic issues, reporting solutions, hosting community events, and amplifying local actions. Topics range from housing to mental health to food insecurity to elections, and all content is co-produced with community partners. Since 2022, The Green Line has completed 17 action journeys across 58 Toronto neighbourhoods. Nearly three-quarters of its audience is under 40 and its creators are mainly Gen Z and millennials, many of whom return again and again – not just as attendees, but as panellists, collaborators, and journalists-in-the-making. The Green Line brings sharper editorial instincts and deeper accountability to the local media landscape. In three years its approach has inspired 30 other newsrooms, earned national recognition, and achieved 48% revenue growth – all while resisting cynicism and rebuilding social trust.

In Calgary’s Beltline neighbourhood, students from Connaught School helped reimagine their daily journey to school, transforming a street near a hazardous intersection into a vibrant, child-friendly space. Through a partnership between Sustainable Calgary and Everactive Schools, the [Connaught Open Street](https://www.sustainablecalgary.org/projects/cos) project empowered students to assess local safety concerns and co-design solutions that promote walking, wheeling, and well-being. Students identified a nearby intersection with high-speed cut-through traffic as an opportunity for improvement. The resulting project was a street-to-park transformation that calmed traffic, added green space, and created a healthier environment for kids and families. Piloted in 2022 and 2023 with temporary road closures and on-site programming, the initiative quickly gained traction, earning community support, national recognition, and municipal endorsement. In May 2025, Calgary City Council approved the permanent road closure and rezoning, cementing the project as a landmark in youth-driven civic design. The Connaught Open Street now stands as a model for how children’s voices can shape safer, more engaging urban spaces.

While the COVID-19 pandemic amplified social isolation, the problem long predates it – and has persisted even as restrictions have been lifted. [Rx for Social Connection](https://thebentway.ca/publication/rx-for-social-connection/) is an applied research project that used The Bentway, a revitalized public space under the Gardiner Expressway in Toronto, as a living lab to examine how “softer” city-building strategies – prioritizing care, repair, intimacy, and co-creation – can nurture more socially connected urban environments and combat loneliness. The project focused on The Bentway’s 2024 programming season, which positioned public art and shared spaces as case studies for urban research, using public life observation, public health surveys, and expert interviews. The project invited participants to reflect on public space design and programming, along with the role they play in fostering social connection. The study demonstrated that public spaces are powerful public health tools that encourage connection, reduce loneliness, and promote well-being. As the population’s health needs evolve, public space design and programming should be recognized as essential interventions – ones that invite people to gather, linger, and feel that they matter.

Government Street, one of the most visited public places in Victoria, remains strongly defined by its colonial history, with little acknowledgement of the Songhees and Esquimalt Nations whose unceded territories the city occupies. The City of Victoria is working to repair that narrative, incorporating Indigenous language, culture, and history into the space to make it more welcoming and to foster a sense of belonging and recognition for Indigenous peoples. Rather than a fixed plan or timeline, the [Government Street Refresh](https://engage.victoria.ca/government-street-refresh) initiative envisions long-term, incremental transformation through collaboration, experimentation, and investment. Current efforts include introducing car-free zones – some timed, some permanent – for outdoor seating and cultural programming; co-developing, with the Songhees and Esquimalt Nations, a cultural interpretive strategy and a set of guiding principles for reconciliation-based public-realm design; and advancing detailed design for two flexible pedestrian-priority blocks that incorporate plantings and trees, reflecting Indigenous cultural expression at the site. Together, these efforts signal a shift toward a more inclusive and responsive urban landscape – one that honours Indigenous presence, invites shared stewardship, and reimagines Government Street as a place for the whole community.

[Jane’s Walk](https://janeswalk.org/) is a global festival of walking conversations that are led by local residents, creating spaces for people to share stories, ideas, and insights about the places they live, work, and play. Started in Toronto in 2007 and named after urbanist Jane Jacobs, who advocated walking through cities to understand how people lived and created communities within them, the organization continues her legacy of curiosity. Jane’s Walks, which are free, reconnect people and places by creating spaces for residents to share their passion for and knowledge about the cities they live in. Held annually on the first weekend of May, the community-led festival fosters civic dialogue, trust, and connection in an increasingly fragmented urban landscape. In 2025, the festival included 158 walks in Toronto – among thousands of walks in the 500 cities that have participated – reaching up to 5,000 participants across the city. Survey results showed that nearly all participants engaged actively in discussions, felt a greater sense of belonging, and felt more connected to the city. These outcomes show a strong appetite for meaningful civic engagement and community dialogue. Jane’s Walk empowers city residents to explore, reflect, and connect, recognizing that everyone is an expert in their own experience and has a role in shaping the city they call home.
City of New Westminster and Simon Fraser University
Burnaby, Gibsons, and New Westminster, BC

Strong democratic institutions bring together residents, decision-makers, and civil society to co-create solutions that reflect public needs, uphold shared values, and encourage action within real-world constraints. Canada is an innovator in creating a new type of collective policy-making: the [citizens’ assembly](https://participedia.net/method/citizens-assembly), first held in 2004 in British Columbia to evaluate a provincial electoral reform proposal, and since scaled nationally with support from Simon Fraser University (SFU). Citizens’ assemblies recruit diverse participants through civic lotteries and engage them in learning and deliberation to craft policy recommendations. While their input is typically not binding, decision-makers are often sponsors of the process and offer a formal response to the public, including rationales for why recommendations were or were not followed – thus bringing citizens closer to the process of making the policies that affect them. Recent years have seen a “deliberative wave” of hundreds of assemblies worldwide, including dozens across Canada. After a pilot facilitated by the SFU Centre for Dialogue in 2024, Canada’s first permanent assembly was established, in [the City of New Westminster](https://www.sfu.ca/dialogue/news/2025/newwest-renews-assembly.html), B.C. It brought together 36 residents over the course of a year to provide recommendations on municipal priorities – and was renewed in 2025 after an evaluation process led by researchers at SFU. Citizens’ assemblies offer a scalable and effective model for collaborative public engagement, leading to enhanced trust, democratic resilience, and social cohesion.

[Synapcity](https://synapcity.ca/), a non-profit focused on civic connection and community action, launched the Pulses program to help strengthen Ottawa’s civic fabric and give people opportunities to socialize with neighbours through regular, facilitated, in-person conversations. The program operates with a chapter-based model similar to that of Scouts and Guides, providing an avenue for hyper-local dialogue and creating welcoming spaces where residents can connect, flex their civic muscles, and engage meaningfully with their communities. The program began in summer 2025 in partnership with the Ottawa Public Library, which has an existing network of spaces to meet. Priorities evolved organically based on the participants in each individual chapter, with tailored outcomes for each group. One embraced themes of civic action and is now working on launching local initiatives in their neighbourhood, while another prioritized the notion of deep dialogue and developed a civics book club. Moving forward, a program to train group leaders in facilitation techniques is in the works (pending funding) and will enable to program to scale as a sandbox for civic curiosity, sparking vibrant conversations across Ottawa and nurturing a more connected, resilient city.

The [East Scarborough Storefront](https://www.thestorefront.org/what-we-do) is a community hub in east Toronto that responds to local challenges in a comprehensive way. Its [Connected Community Approach](https://schoolofcities.utoronto.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/CityResearchInsights_v1.1.pdf) (CCA) helps create the conditions for transformative change with, and in, communities. Developed over 25 years, CCA is a model that works to remove barriers to opportunity, build capacity, and respond to community problems with solutions that are grounded in local contexts. Rather than focusing on isolated programs, CCA at The Storefront nurtures the conditions for collaboration, civic trust, and community-led resilience in responding to various challenges, from climate change to food insecurity to the need for public spaces. For example, food security projects include the Food for Good project to improve resilience and equity in the local food system; a community garden; and the Eco-Food Hub, where resident leaders served 10,000 meals in 2023. The Storefront is a connector, a communicator, and a convenor: it referred over 8,800 people to community resources in 2023, and facilitates partnerships among over 90 local leaders, non-profits, governments, and institutions, including Native Child and Family Services, East Scarborough Boys and Girls Club, University of Toronto Scarborough, and the Toronto Zoo. The CCA lens is now being applied to procurement, supply chains, and arts and culture. This approach offers a powerful alternative to fragmented systems, showing what’s possible when communities are connected, trusted, and empowered.
Ottawa, Renfrew, Lanark, and Prescott-Russell, ON

[United for All](https://www.unitedwayeo.ca/get-involved/united-for-all/) is a United Way initiative to address systemic issues fueling discrimination and division in Ottawa at a time when incidents of hate, racism, and discrimination have risen steadily in the city over the past five years. An estimated 78% of hate incidents across Canada go unreported, suggesting that many people remain uncomfortable using formal reporting processes and highlighting the need for alternative responses to hate. Established in 2016, United for All brings together a wide network of social service agencies, faith groups, human rights organizations, policy-makers, educators, health providers, grassroots activists, and cultural groups to coordinate action against hate, violence, and extremism. Recent initiatives include partnering with the Ottawa Police Service to secure funding for work addressing antisemitism, Islamophobia, misogyny, anti-Black racism, and anti-2SLGBTQ+ hate; hosting community dialogues to navigate geopolitical tensions; and supporting refugee resettlement. It also delivers Upstander training to community leaders to strengthen the capacity of individuals to recognize and respond to hate and discrimination incidents when they happen. Meetings, events, and training sessions have reached full capacity, demonstrating a strong collective commitment to fostering inclusion, safety, and belonging across Ottawa. United for All continues to harness this momentum to build stronger, united communities.
Building community wealth through employment and procurement

[CleanStart](https://cleanstartbc.ca/) is a property maintenance service company that grew out of a waste collection and removal project in Vancouver’s Downtown Eastside. It now provides stable and dignified work to individuals with lived experience of homelessness, poverty, or addiction, all of which can make finding and holding a job more challenging. CleanStart works with non-profit housing providers, property managers, construction companies, and residential clients to provide junk removal, pest control, and cleaning services. The jobs at CleanStart pay a living wage, include extended health benefits, and provide on-the-job training. Its workforce model is rooted in community understanding and is designed to be flexible to accommodate employees’ abilities and schedules. Through its leadership in social procurement, CleanStart generated over $420,000 in social return on employment in 2024.
