This figure accounts for the quantitative value of social impact created from the company’s hiring practices, which have resulted in over 50% of its workforce being made up of individuals who experience moderate to severe barriers to traditional employment. For example, over 40% of their staff have experienced homelessness, 20% identify as First Nations, Metis, or Inuit, and 20% identify as 2SLGBTQ+. Over half of their staff have reported that secure employment with CleanStart has significantly improved their housing situation, illustrating the wide-ranging impact of employment support.

Through its [WorkFirst](https://www.goodwillindustries.ca/power-of-work/) program, Goodwill Industries provides supportive employment for people experiencing difficulties finding or maintaining a job. This means that, in addition to employment opportunities, they provide services like coaching and mentorship that help people find and then keep jobs in the face of barriers such as poverty, physical disability, mental illness or addiction, lack of language skills, low education or work experience, and competing responsibilities like caregiving at home. Employees are hired in positions within the Goodwill social enterprise itself through its network of donation centres, community stores, boutique stores, bookstores, cafes, career centres, and Goodwill Business Solutions services, and paid a competitive wage. Both full- and part-time employees have access to health and dental benefits, skills development, and coaching in life, financial, and career skills. Through its “second chance” policy, Goodwill helps every employee develop both a Career Plan and a Life Plan to help them overcome the challenges they are experiencing in any aspect of their life and build a lasting career. In this way, the WorkFirst program sets up all employees with both the confidence and the wraparound services they need to succeed in their careers.

The [Inclusive Local Economic Opportunity Initiative](https://www.unitedwaygt.org/our-work/ileo-initiative/) (ILEO), a collaborative model convened by the United Way Greater Toronto and BMO Financial Group, brings together the private, public, and community sectors to find innovative ways to reduce economic gaps at the neighbourhood level. The first focus neighbourhood is the Greater Golden Mile in Scarborough, which is expecting to see rapid commercial and residential development as the three major transit projects within its borders are completed, and where many residents earn less than the city’s median income. Among the ILEO’s initiatives to support economic development there is the Storefront Starter Golden Mile, a free three-phase program that helps new and aspiring entrepreneurs launch or scale their ideas through business training, access to startup capital, and relationship building with large corporations within the ILEO network. The program provides business owners with market and retail opportunities in prime locations around Toronto, including the Distillery District and the Yonge Eglinton Centre. Another initiative is ILEO’s Construction Union Employment Pathway, which is a six-week program that helps marginalized, low-income residents in the Greater Golden Mile enter the construction trades. Participants are trained and given paid placements on construction projects locally and across the GTA, and provided with wraparound support services and mentorship. As the Greater Golden Mile evolves, ILEO’s model offers a locally rooted model for building opportunity, resilience, and shared prosperity.

The Toronto neighbourhoods of Regent Park, Moss Park, and St. James Town are home to many new Canadians and a large youth population. Seeing the potential of peer support to ease the transition into life in Canada, the non-profit [Happy Mom Happy Children](https://www.happymomhappychildren.com/) employs local youth to help children achieve academic success and help newcomer families navigate life and school. Through their Tutoring and Youth Employment Program, they train local youth tutors (aged 13 to 29) to provide academic tutoring for children in the community (aged 4 to 12). The paid youth tutors receive mentorship, leadership training, and workshops on relevant subjects like communication, child engagement, and career development. For many young people this is their first job, which they use as a stepping stone to develop their careers. Many return to mentor or train new youth tutors. In 2024/25 alone, 63 youth were trained as tutors, who in turn tutored 127 students. Happy Mom Happy Children also provides services that bring mothers together, such as their Let’s Eat Healthy cooking classes, their Let’s Hit the Gym fitness classes, and their Grab a Book & Join Us reading program for mothers and children. By nurturing local youth, Happy Mom Happy Children is creating a cycle of mutual care and expertise that enriches the entire community across multiple generations.
Organizing for a Community Benefit Agreement

Big changes, including a subway station on the future Ontario Line, are in the works for Toronto’s Moss Park neighbourhood. Major public and private investments will bring not only subway access but park revitalization, a new recreation centre, and dozens of private sector housing developments. Moss Park is one of Toronto’s lowest income neighbourhoods, with a high number of recent immigrants. In response to this planned rapid development, a group of residents, community organizations, and service providers formed the [Moss Park Coalition](https://www.empowermosspark.ca/) to advocate for a CBA for the Moss Park Station project in order to ensure the community takes part in shaping these developments – and that it benefits from them. Through community engagement efforts, with the support of the University of Toronto’s Housing Justice Lab in 2024/25, the Coalition issued a report identifying several top issues for residents: affordable housing, tenant protection, food access, and local employment. This report has become an essential tool in the efforts to put pressure on government officials for a CBA that will help the community address their priorities. The Moss Park Coalition has organized across the community and built grassroots capacity to advocate for – and steer the future of – the neighbourhood, in particular fighting against displacement so residents can live well and keep their community in place.
Building a thriving local food system

[Fireweed Food Co-op](https://www.fireweedfoodcoop.ca/) (FFC) is a non-profit co-op based in Winnipeg for producers and consumers of food that is grown sustainably in Manitoba. FFC supports the development of a short-chain regional food system that is more resilient to disruptions and can respond to changing conditions more quickly than a globalized supply chain, and that engages everyone from farmers to eaters. It operates three connected projects that strengthen the local food system: the South Osborne Farmers' Market, Fireweed Food Hub, and Fireweed Veggie Van. Since it began in 2016, the South Osborne Farmers' Market has grown to become the second-largest farmers' market in Winnipeg. The Food Hub is Winnipeg’s first cooperatively run aggregator and wholesale distributor of food. Sourcing from over 35 local producers, it provides a competitive alternative to the global supply chain by making it easier for wholesale customers to source locally. The Veggie Van is the most recent venture: a mobile market that distributes fresh fruits and veggies in communities with few fresh food options throughout Winnipeg using a pay-what-you-can model, thus removing common barriers – location and affordability – and increasing food security. These projects contribute to a thriving local food system that keeps more dollars in the local economy, builds important community connections and reduces food waste.

The [Good Greens Food Reclamation Program](https://www.downtownwindsor.ca/goodgreens/) operates in partnership with the Downtown Windsor Farmers’ Market to address the dual issues of food waste and food insecurity in Windsor’s urban core. At the close of each Saturday market, Good Greens purchases unsold produce, baked goods, and preserves from local vendors at 20–80% below retail prices. These goods are then weighed and sorted by a team of (primarily youth) volunteers and redistributed that same afternoon to a network of seven downtown-based shelters and social service organizations, many of whom rely on food donations to meet rising demand with limited funding. Since launching in October 2023, the program has reclaimed over 7,500 kilograms of locally grown fruits and vegetables, 5,200 baked goods, and 47 litres of preserves. These goods have contributed to more than 18,000 meals served through distributor partners, reaching many individuals living in Windsor’s downtown, where food can be difficult to access. With a redistribution success rate over 97%, the program has prevented thousands of kilograms of CO₂ emissions in 2024 by diverting food from landfills, avoiding the need to produce more food in replacement. By reclaiming surplus food from the Downtown Windsor Farmers’ Market and redistributing it to front-line organizations, the program not only nourishes thousands of residents in Windsor’s urban core but also champions environmental sustainability.

Located in Toronto’s East End, [Nourish East End](https://nourisheastend.ca/community-dinners/) is a market-style food bank that runs a community dinner on the fourth Monday of every month, a longstanding tradition that predates the food bank itself. The dinners began as a collective effort in recognition of the challenges experienced by many people in the community living in poverty and experiencing food insecurity and social isolation. The Community Dinner Program strives to address these issues by providing meaningful social interaction in the company of neighbours and friends while sharing hot, nutritious, and culturally diverse meals in a safe and welcoming space. After dinner, guests are invited to a “Gab & Games” social event. Along with a chance to chat and play games over snacks, it features a resource table and a referral service that assists community members seeking access to local resources. These dinners are run by volunteers and use an innovative sponsorship model where organizations can sponsor a dinner either by providing a donation or by hosting the dinner – including planning, paying for, and cooking the meal as well as providing volunteers to help with serving. In a city where food insecurity and social isolation often go hand in hand, Nourish East End’s community dinner model offers a reliable and warm respite, one meal at a time.

[Not Far From The Tree](https://notfarfromthetree.org/) (NFFTT) harvests and shares fruit from trees in Toronto – trees that constitute an “urban orchard” producing over 1.5 million pounds of fruit on city property and over 6 million on private property. Much of this fruit is left to rot each year, creating food waste and adding the emissions equivalent of burning 1.5 million pounds of coal. Since 2008, NFFTT has picked and shared over 280,000 pounds of fruit, splitting the harvest three ways: a third to the tree owner, a third to volunteers, and a third donated to community agency partners. Over 97,000 pounds of fruit were donated to these 70-plus partners, which include shelters, food banks, community fridges, and housing and meal programs. Every year, NFFTT mobilizes over 1,000 volunteers to pick fruit throughout the summer and early fall. They also steward the health of the urban orchard by registering trees, planting new trees, and caring for older ones. Through the power of fruit trees, Not Far From The Tree and its community of volunteers and tree owners nurture sustainable and connected communities across Toronto that can enjoy their urban orchard for generations to come.

In the City of Vaughan, north of Toronto, a community of neighbours living around [Marita Payne Park](https://maritapaynepark.ca/) worked with the municipal government to create new opportunities for both resident engagement and urban agriculture in this vibrant green space. They piloted a food forest in the park with edible and pollinator-friendly plantings, with the Friends of Marita Payne Park group forming to steward it. The community then created a [vision](https://maritapaynepark.ca/vision/) for the initiative’s future in which the park will become a year-round hub for nature-based learning and connection through outdoor programming like story walks, meditation, and art shows. In this vision, the food forest will continue to provide community members with free access to fruit trees, herbs, and shrubs while improving the park’s biodiversity (for example, adding bird and bat boxes), as well as being a place for people to foster friendships and knowledge about food forest stewardship. The park could also become a place to pilot new technologies, like a tool that uses AI, geographic information systems (GIS), and publicly available datasets to help the City track carbon sequestering in its green spaces, and educational apps and nest cams that would engage young people in the environment. The Marita Payne Park project is an ever-growing pilot that serves as a model for reimagining a park as a living hub for nature, innovation, and community.

Since 2021, Malvern Family Resource Centre (MFRC) has led the [Malvern Urban Farm](https://mfrc.org/community-and-family-programs/food-justice-in-malvern/), an urban agriculture project located under power lines along the Finch hydro corridor in Scarborough, in eastern Toronto. Seventeen farmers each maintain a plot on the urban farm. Together, they have produced over 120,000 pounds of culturally relevant produce – like callaloo, a staple of Caribbean cuisine – and launched 16 small businesses through their urban agriculture skills development lab, as well as supporting many underemployed and low-income residents in the community. Beyond food production, MFRC uses the farm to encourage community engagement through youth training, farm camp programs, and volunteering. In 2024, the Resource Center expanded its farmers' market, increasing vendor participation and food access. It also introduced “Market Bucks” – discreet tokens for low-income families – which successfully supported 200 households and generated a 37% increase in market sales. MFRC continues to expand, recently receiving City approval to add an additional acre under the hydroelectric lines to its farm. Starting in 2025, the Center has also been working with organizations in the neighbouring communities of Agincourt, West Hill, Scarborough Village, Morningside, and Kingston-Galloway as they launch their own community farms. The Malvern Urban Farm demonstrates how underutilized land can be put to productive, community-focused use, supporting neighbourhood food sovereignty, economic opportunity, and resilience.
